5.overview:
The first verse builds a monument — commander of the army, a great man, in high favour, a mighty man of valour — and knocks it down with three words: but he was a leper. It also says, in passing and as though it were nothing, that by him the LORD had given victory to Syria. Israel's God was running the enemy's campaigns, and one of the things one of those raids brought home was a little Israelite girl.

She is the only evangelist in the chapter. Everything that follows comes out of one sentence she volunteered to the woman who owned her — and by the time it has climbed the chain of command it is a king-to-king letter with three quarters of a ton of silver attached and no prophet in it at all. Elisha will not come to the door, will not perform the ceremony Naaman had scripted on the road from Damascus, and sends a messenger to tell him to wash in a muddy border river seven times.

He comes up clean, with skin like the flesh of a little child — the writer's own words for the girl in verse 2 — and goes home a believer with muddled theology, an honest conscience and a question about the temple of Rimmon. And a servant who had watched the whole thing runs down the road after him to sell what had just been given away free.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — But He Was a Leper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything in the first verse builds — commander of the army, a great man, in high favour, a mighty man of valour — and then one word takes it all down: but he was a leper (v. 1). And the verse says something else in passing that ought to stop the reader: by him the LORD had given victory to Syria. A little Israelite girl, carried off in a Syrian raid and working in his wife's household, says the sentence the chapter turns on: would that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! (v. 3). It goes up the chain to the king, who sends a letter and ten talents of silver — and the king of Israel tears his clothes and says am I God, to kill and to make alive?, certain it is a pretext for war (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's God was handing victories to Israel's enemy, through a general who did not know his name — possibly including the very raid that took the girl. God was running that army's campaigns and one of its spoils was the child who would tell its commander where to be healed.
verseByVerse.examples: And watch the address get lost. She said the prophet who is in Samaria. By the time the request reaches the top it is a state letter from one king to another with no prophet in it at all, and the king of Israel — who has a prophet four streets away — can think of nothing but diplomacy. Power talks to power, and mislays the address a slave girl had exactly right.

verseByVerse.quote: Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master and in high favor, because by him the LORD had given victory to Syria. He was a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. Now the Syrians on one of their raids had carried off a little girl from the land of Israel, and she worked in the service of Naaman's wife. She said to her mistress, "Would that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! He would cure him of his leprosy." So Naaman went in and told his lord, "Thus and so spoke the girl from the land of Israel." And the king of Syria said, "Go now, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel." So he went, taking with him ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, and ten changes of clothing. And he brought the letter to the king of Israel, which read, "When this letter reaches you, know that I have sent to you Naaman my servant, that you may cure him of his leprosy." And when the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and said, "Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man sends word to me to cure a man of his leprosy? Only consider, and see how he is seeking a quarrel with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master and in high favor, because by him the LORD had given victory to Syria. He was a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper.'

Read the verse as it is built, because it is built to fall over at the end.

Commander of the army. A great man with his master. In high favour. A mighty man of valour. Four commendations, each one solid, the sort of sentence a state funeral is built out of.

And then: but he was a leper.

Everybody has a clause on the other side of that but, and most people's is not visible from the outside. His was on his skin. The Hebrew word covers a range of skin diseases and not only what we call leprosy today, and plainly it had not put him out of society — he commands an army and stands in front of a king, which he could not have done in Israel, where such a man went outside the camp (Lev. 13). But it was there every morning, and no amount of favour touched it.

Now the clause in the middle, which is the most startling thing in the chapter and is dropped in as if it were nothing. By him the LORD had given victory to Syria.

Not Rimmon. Not Syrian arms. The God of Israel handed victories to the enemy of Israel, through a pagan general who had never heard of him, and the writer of Kings mentions it in a subordinate clause on the way to something else.

He is running that army's campaigns. And one of the things that army came home with, on one of those raids that the LORD gave them, was a little girl.

'Now the Syrians on one of their raids had carried off a little girl from the land of Israel, and she worked in the service of Naaman's wife.'

Count what has been taken from her. Her home, her country, her parents, her freedom, and her name — the writer never gives it, and probably nobody in that house asked for it either. She was stolen in a border raid, of the kind that carried off livestock and children in the same afternoon, and she is now domestic staff in the house of the man whose army did it.

'She said to her mistress, "Would that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! He would cure him of his leprosy."'

That is what she does with it.

She had every reason on earth to say nothing. She had better reason still to be quietly glad about the disease — that a man who raided her village is rotting is not an unnatural thing for a kidnapped child to feel. What she says instead, to her mistress, in the enemy's language, in the enemy's house, is: there is a man in my country who could heal him.

She is a slave, a child, a foreigner and a woman, which in that world is four separate reasons for her opinion to count for nothing, and she is the only person in the chapter who does any evangelism.

She is also not asked. Nobody consulted her; she volunteered it into a conversation with the woman who owned her. And she never appears again. The greatest thing that happened to that household happened because of her, and the text does not record that anybody told her how it turned out.

Most of what God does through ordinary Christians is like that. One sentence, said to somebody in your own house, about what you happen to know — and no way of finding out for years, or at all, what became of it.

'So Naaman went in and told his lord, "Thus and so spoke the girl from the land of Israel."'

'And the king of Syria said, "Go now, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel." So he went, taking with him ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, and ten changes of clothing.'

Now watch the message travel up the chain and lose the one thing that mattered in it.

The girl said the prophet who is in Samaria. Naaman reports it to the king. The king's response is to write to the king of Israel — because in his world a thing like this is transacted between crowns, and if there is a wonder-worker in Samaria then obviously he belongs to the palace.

The letter that arrives contains no prophet at all.

The freight is enormous. Ten talents of silver is something like three quarters of a ton; six thousand shekels of gold; ten changes of clothing, which in that economy are capital goods. A column of it, on the road, to buy a cure.

'And he brought the letter to the king of Israel, which read, "When this letter reaches you, know that I have sent to you Naaman my servant, that you may cure him of his leprosy."'

'And when the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and said, "Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man sends word to me to cure a man of his leprosy? Only consider, and see how he is seeking a quarrel with me."'

He is right about the theology and wrong about everything else.

Am I God, to kill and to make alive? He is not, and he is quoting Scripture without knowing it — I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal (Deut. 32:39). That much is sound.

What he cannot do is take the next step. There is a prophet in his kingdom. That prophet has raised a dead child, healed a poisoned spring and fed a hundred men, and everybody in the country appears to know where he lives except the king, who tears his clothes and starts calculating how Syria intends to use this as a pretext for invasion.

It is chapter one's question again, and it has now been asked of a whole succession of these men. Is there no God in Israel? There is, and the throne cannot remember him.

'But when Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, he sent to the king, saying, "Why have you torn your clothes? Let him come now to me, that he may know that there is a prophet in Israel."'

There is the sentence the chapter exists for. Not that he may be cured, though he will be. That he may know that there is a prophet in Israel.

The healing is a means. What is at stake is whether a Syrian field marshal goes home knowing whose country he has been raiding.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elisha sends word: let him come now to me, that he may know that there is a prophet in Israel (v. 8). So a column of horses and chariots pulls up outside a house — and the prophet does not come out. A messenger relays seven words of instruction: go and wash in the Jordan seven times (v. 10). Naaman is enraged, and says exactly why: behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me and stand and call upon the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the place (v. 11), and besides, the rivers of Damascus are better water (v. 12). His servants talk him down with an argument he cannot answer (v. 13), and he goes down and dips seven times, and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: He had the whole ceremony written before he arrived: the prophet emerges, stands, invokes the name, waves a hand over the spot. He is not angry at being refused — he is being healed — he is angry at being healed the wrong way. The offence is to his script.
verseByVerse.examples: And the Jordan is not medicine. His objection is factually correct: Abana and Pharpar run clear off the snows of Hermon and the lower Jordan is a brown ditch. What the Jordan is, is the border — the river Israel crossed to come into the land. He is being asked to go down into the water of the people he has spent his career raiding, and to come up out of it six times still a leper before anything happens at all.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, he sent to the king, saying, "Why have you torn your clothes? Let him come now to me, that he may know that there is a prophet in Israel." So Naaman came with his horses and chariots and stood at the door of Elisha's house. And Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, "Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall be restored, and you shall be clean." But Naaman was angry and went away, saying, "Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me and stand and call upon the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the place and cure the leper. Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Could I not wash in them and be clean?" So he turned and went away in a rage. But his servants came near and said to him, "My father, it is a great word the prophet has spoken to you; will you not do it? Has he actually said to you, 'Wash, and be clean'?" So he went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Naaman came with his horses and chariots and stood at the door of Elisha's house.'

Picture it from the street. A column of chariots, cavalry, a general in his armour and three quarters of a ton of silver, drawn up in a residential lane in Samaria, outside somebody's front door.

'And Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, "Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall be restored, and you shall be clean."'

He does not come out.

The most powerful soldier in Syria is standing on his step and Elisha sends a servant to the door with a sentence. There is no interview, no examination, no laying on of hands and no meeting of any kind. The man never sees him.

That is deliberate, and the next verse tells us exactly what it cost.

'But Naaman was angry and went away, saying, "Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me and stand and call upon the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the place and cure the leper.'

I thought. He had it written.

Listen to how detailed the script is. The prophet comes out — to me, in person. He stands. He calls on the name of his God, out loud. He waves his hand over the place. And then the cure. Naaman had rehearsed that scene on the road from Damascus, probably for days, and what he got was a messenger at a door telling him to go and take a bath.

Be precise about what he is angry at, because it is not what people usually assume. He has not been refused. He has been promised a complete cure, free, on the spot. He is furious because it is being done the wrong way — without ceremony, without deference, and without him.

Here is a question to put to yourself, and it is one of the more searching ones in the Old Testament. How much of your disappointment with God is actually disappointment that he did not do it the way you had pictured? Not that the prayer went unanswered — that the answer arrived through an ordinary person, or a long dull process, or a piece of advice from somebody junior to you, instead of the way you had staged it in your mind.

'Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Could I not wash in them and be clean?" So he turned and went away in a rage.'

Here he is simply correct.

The Abana comes down off the snows of Hermon and runs clear and cold through Damascus, and the Pharpar likewise. The Jordan south of Galilee is a slow brown thing between mud banks. As a proposition about water, his objection is unanswerable, and any Syrian would have said the same.

That is exactly the point, because the Jordan is not being offered as a treatment. Nothing in that river is good for skin. The Jordan is the border. It is the water Israel crossed to come into the land, and the water that opened for Elijah and Elisha in the last chapter but one, and it is the one river in the region that means something rather than does something.

He is being asked to go down into the water of the people he has spent his career raiding, seven times, in front of his own staff, and to come up out of it six times unchanged.

Take that last detail seriously, because it is where most people give up. There is no gradual improvement described. He goes under and comes up a leper, and does it again, and again. Five times he has obeyed and there is nothing to show for it, and the men holding his clothes are watching.

'But his servants came near and said to him, "My father, it is a great word the prophet has spoken to you; will you not do it? Has he actually said to you, 'Wash, and be clean'?"'

His own staff talk him out of it, and the argument they use is a good one.

If he had told you to do something enormous, they say, you would have done it without blinking. You would have marched an army, paid a fortune, gone on a pilgrimage. He asked you to do something small, and the smallness is the only thing you are objecting to.

Notice their nerve as well as their logic. These are junior men addressing a raging general, and they open with my father — the affectionate form, the thing you say to a man you serve and also love. They handle him beautifully.

This is the second time in one chapter that Naaman is saved by somebody beneath him. A captive child told him where to go; his own servants get him into the water. The great man is carried the entire distance by people whose names the record does not keep.

'So he went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.'

He goes down.

The armour comes off in front of his men, and the commander of the army of Syria wades into a muddy Israelite river and puts his head under it seven times, and comes up clean.

Now look at the phrase the writer chooses for the healed skin: like the flesh of a little child. The Hebrew is na'ar qaton.

And go back to verse 2, and the girl. She is a na'arah qetannah — the identical words, in the feminine. A little girl.

His flesh came up out of that water like the flesh of the child who told him where to go. The writer has closed the circle with two words, and said nothing about it, and left it there for anybody reading slowly.

One more thing before leaving the river, and it is what the Lord Jesus did with this chapter. Preaching in his home synagogue at Nazareth, he told his neighbours that there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian (Luke 4:27). He had already said the same thing about the widow at Zarephath.

Many lepers in Israel. Covenant lepers, with the promises and the law and the temple, in the prophet's own country — and God healed the enemy commander. That was his text, and the congregation drove him out of the town and tried to throw him off a cliff for it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — Two Mule Loads of Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He comes back a believer: behold, I know that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel (v. 15) — which is exactly what Elisha said the visit was for. The gift is refused under oath and refused again when pressed (v. 16). So Naaman asks for two mule loads of Israelite soil, because he intends to sacrifice to no other god ever again and thinks he needs the right ground to do it on (v. 17). And then he raises, himself, the one thing that will not fit: his duty is to support his king's arm in the temple of Rimmon, and when the king bows he bows. The LORD pardon your servant in this matter (v. 18). Elisha says three words: go in peace (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The gift is refused so that nobody can go home having bought it. A talent of silver would have made the whole thing a transaction between a rich foreigner and a useful holy man, and Naaman would have carried his cure home as something he had paid a fair price for. Nine verses later a man will sell it to him after all.
verseByVerse.examples: And Naaman's theology is still half pagan — he thinks the God of Israel needs Israelite dirt under the altar — while his devotion is entirely real. Elisha does not examine him on it. He does not license the business in Rimmon's temple either, or forbid it. He sends a brand-new believer away in peace with a tender conscience and leaves God to do the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and he came and stood before him. And he said, "Behold, I know that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel; so accept now a present from your servant." But he said, "As the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none." And he urged him to take it, but he refused. Then Naaman said, "If not, please let there be given to your servant two mule loads of earth, for from now on your servant will not offer burnt offering or sacrifice to any god but the LORD. In this matter may the LORD pardon your servant: when my master goes into the house of Rimmon to worship there, leaning on my arm, and I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, when I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, the LORD pardon your servant in this matter." He said to him, "Go in peace." But when Naaman had gone from him a short distance,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then he returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and he came and stood before him. And he said, "Behold, I know that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel; so accept now a present from your servant."'

He brings the whole column back — a journey of some fifty miles each way — to say one sentence to a man who would not come to the door for him.

The sentence itself is a confession of faith. There is no God in all the earth but in Israel. That is not a compliment to a local deity; it is a denial of every god he has ever served, made by the commander of the armies of a country whose state god is Rimmon.

Verse 8 said the visit was so that he may know that there is a prophet in Israel. He has gone considerably further than that.

'But he said, "As the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none." And he urged him to take it, but he refused.'

Elijah's oath again, and a flat refusal, repeated when pressed.

Understand why, because Elisha is not being precious about money — the man lives on gifts from farmers and eats at a woman's table in Shunem. He refuses this one because of what it would make the healing into.

If Naaman pays, then Naaman goes home with something he purchased. The whole transaction becomes a rich foreigner and a useful holy man settling on a price, and everything the chapter has been doing — the girl, the muddy river, the messenger at the door, the six pointless dips — is undone at the last minute by an invoice.

Grace that can be paid for is not grace, and the prophet will not allow the question to remain open. Nine verses from now, someone will settle it for a fee behind his back.

'Then Naaman said, "If not, please let there be given to your servant two mule loads of earth, for from now on your servant will not offer burnt offering or sacrifice to any god but the LORD.'

What follows is a new believer's theology about four minutes old, and it is a strange mixture.

The commitment is total and unambiguous: no burnt offering, no sacrifice, to any god but the LORD, from now on. He has finished with Rimmon.

The reasoning underneath it is still half pagan. He wants two mule loads of Israelite soil to take home, because he assumes the God of Israel is attached to the ground of Israel, and that to build a proper altar in Damascus he will need to stand it on a patch of the right country. It is the territorial thinking of the age — the same instinct as Syrian officers deciding that the LORD is a god of the hills but not the valleys (1 Kgs. 20:23).

Elisha does not correct him.

Sit with that, because the temptation with a new convert is exactly the opposite. Here is a man whose doctrine of God is muddled in a way anybody could see, and who is about to build an altar on imported dirt, and the prophet lets him go home with it. What is right in him is the thing that matters and it is entirely right: he will sacrifice to nobody else. The rest will get sorted out, and it will not be sorted out by an examination on the day of his conversion.

'In this matter may the LORD pardon your servant: when my master goes into the house of Rimmon to worship there, leaning on my arm, and I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, when I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, the LORD pardon your servant in this matter."'

This is the difficult verse, and it should be handled slowly and without pretending it is easy.

Rimmon is the Syrian storm god. Naaman's office includes being the arm the king leans on, physically, in the temple — and when the king goes down, the man supporting him goes down with him. It is a posture of state, not a private devotion, and he cannot resign the duty without resigning the office.

Now notice four things about how he raises it.

He raises it himself. Nobody asked. He has just walked out of the river and made his confession, and the first thing he does with his new faith is go looking through his own diary for what will not fit.

He describes the act exactly, three times over in one verse, without softening the words. He does not say attend a ceremony or accompany the king. He says I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, and then says it again, and again.

Permission is not what he asks for. He asks pardon — which is an admission that the thing needs pardoning.

He is not, in any case, asking to worship Rimmon. He has just renounced every sacrifice to every other god in the previous sentence. What he is describing is a bodily posture in the course of a duty, and he is asking mercy for it in advance because he knows how it looks and cannot see a way out.

'He said to him, "Go in peace." But when Naaman had gone from him a short distance,'

Three words, and Elisha neither licenses it nor forbids it.

Do not turn go in peace into a ruling in either direction; it is a dismissal, the ordinary Hebrew farewell, and the writer plainly declines to settle the case for us. What Elisha does is let a four-minute-old believer go home with a tender conscience, an honest question and God to work on him.

That is where the passage is most useful. A man who names his one compromise out loud on the first day, in plain words, and asks God to pardon it, is in an incomparably better condition than a long-standing believer who has stopped noticing his. The danger is never the compromise you are troubled about. It is the one that has gone quiet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: See, my master has spared this Naaman the Syrian — and Gehazi swears by the covenant name that he will run after him and get something (v. 20). The lie he tells is plausible ministry business: two young men have just arrived from the hill country of Ephraim and need a talent of silver and two changes of clothing (v. 22). Naaman is delighted, presses two talents on him, and sends two of his own servants to carry it (v. 23). Then: where have you been, Gehazi? — your servant went nowhere (v. 25). And the sentence: the leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your descendants forever, and he goes out a leper, like snow (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Elisha's question in verse 26 names six things Gehazi never touched — olive orchards, vineyards, sheep, oxen, male and female servants — because he is not describing the theft but the plan. Silver becomes land, and land becomes flocks, and flocks become households. He saw the whole staircase, and he saw the timing: was it a time to sell, to the one Gentile in the book who had just learned that God's mercy cannot be bought, the thing he had just been told was free.
verseByVerse.examples: And the disease does not vanish; it changes address. Gehazi took Naaman's silver and got Naaman's leprosy, and the chapter that opened with a captive girl who had nothing and gave away the best thing she knew closes with a servant who had everything and sold it.

verseByVerse.quote: Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, "See, my master has spared this Naaman the Syrian, in not accepting from his hand what he brought. As the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him." So Gehazi followed Naaman. And when Naaman saw someone running after him, he got down from the chariot to meet him and said, "Is all well?" And he said, "All is well. My master has sent me to say, 'There have just now come to me from the hill country of Ephraim two young men of the sons of the prophets. Please give them a talent of silver and two changes of clothing.'" And Naaman said, "Be pleased to accept two talents." And he urged him and tied up two talents of silver in two bags, with two changes of clothing, and laid them on two of his servants. And they carried them before Gehazi. And when he came to the hill, he took them from their hand and put them in the house, and he sent the men away, and they departed. He went in and stood before his master, and Elisha said to him, "Where have you been, Gehazi?" And he said, "Your servant went nowhere." But he said to him, "Did not my heart go when the man turned from his chariot to meet you? Was it a time to accept money and garments, olive orchards and vineyards, sheep and oxen, male servants and female servants? Therefore the leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your descendants forever." So he went out from his presence a leper, like snow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, "See, my master has spared this Naaman the Syrian, in not accepting from his hand what he brought. As the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him."'

Two things are in that sentence and both are ugly.

This Naaman the Syrian. Not the man who was just healed; not the convert who has confessed that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. A foreigner who has got away with something. The contempt is racial and it is quite unbothered about itself.

Then: as the LORD lives, I will run after him. He swears by the covenant name — the oath his master uses, the oath Elijah used — in order to commit a fraud. He has been standing next to holiness for years and has picked up the vocabulary and nothing else.

'So Gehazi followed Naaman. And when Naaman saw someone running after him, he got down from the chariot to meet him and said, "Is all well?"'

Naaman climbs down off his chariot to meet a servant running up the road. That is a courtesy from a general to a household slave, and it tells you what the last few hours have done to him.

'And he said, "All is well. My master has sent me to say, 'There have just now come to me from the hill country of Ephraim two young men of the sons of the prophets. Please give them a talent of silver and two changes of clothing.'"'

Study the lie, because it is well made.

It is modest — a talent, not ten. It is plausible: the sons of the prophets are real, they are poor, they do arrive, and Elisha does feed them. It accounts for the change of mind without embarrassing his master. And it is charitable in appearance: the money is for two poor students, not for Gehazi.

Frauds inside religious work almost always look like this. Not a raid on the treasury but a small, credible, sympathetic need, invented by somebody with enough inside knowledge to make the details right.

'And Naaman said, "Be pleased to accept two talents." And he urged him and tied up two talents of silver in two bags, with two changes of clothing, and laid them on two of his servants. And they carried them before Gehazi.'

He doubles it, and presses it on him, exactly as he had pressed the gift on Elisha an hour before.

There is something painful in the man's pleasure. He is thrilled to be asked at last. He ties the bags himself, and sends two of his own servants to carry a hundred and fifty pounds of silver up the road in front of a thief, because he thinks he is finally being allowed to give something back.

'And when he came to the hill, he took them from their hand and put them in the house, and he sent the men away, and they departed.'

The last stretch he manages alone. He takes the bags off Naaman's men before they can be seen, sends them away, and puts the silver in the house.

Every detail of that verse is the work of a man who has thought about how not to be caught.

'He went in and stood before his master, and Elisha said to him, "Where have you been, Gehazi?" And he said, "Your servant went nowhere."'

Four words. Your servant went nowhere.

He is standing in front of a man who has known things he was not told all through this book, and he lies to his face about a two-hour absence with the silver still warm in the next room.

'But he said to him, "Did not my heart go when the man turned from his chariot to meet you? Was it a time to accept money and garments, olive orchards and vineyards, sheep and oxen, male servants and female servants?'

Now count the list, because it is longer than the crime.

Gehazi took silver and clothing. Elisha names money and garments — and then olive orchards, vineyards, sheep, oxen, male servants, female servants. Six things that were never in the bags.

He is not describing the theft. He is describing the plan. He can see what that silver was going to become: an estate, with terraces and flocks and a household of servants, and a retired man of God's servant living on it. Gehazi did not want two talents. He wanted a life, and the talents were the first instalment.

Then the phrase that carries the weight of the whole rebuke: was it a time?

Not is it ever right to take money. Elisha lived on the gifts of the faithful. The question is about the hour. At the precise moment when a Gentile soldier was being taught, at some cost, that the mercy of God is not for sale, God's own prophet's servant ran down the road and sold it to him.

Naaman is going to reach Damascus believing something slightly different about Israel's God than he believed on the riverbank, and it will be Gehazi's doing.

'Therefore the leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your descendants forever." So he went out from his presence a leper, like snow.'

The leprosy of Naaman.

Not leprosy in general — his. The disease did not disappear when the Syrian came up out of the Jordan. It changed address. Gehazi went after Naaman's silver and came back with Naaman's skin, and the writer's last three words are among the coldest in the book: a leper, like snow.

The sentence is severe, and the clause about his descendants is severe in a way that troubles modern readers particularly. Two things can honestly be said. Households in that world stood or fell together, and a man who was building an estate for his sons out of stolen money is told that what his sons will actually inherit is the disease. And the writer does not tie it off neatly: three chapters later Gehazi is found in conversation with the king of Israel, telling him about Elisha's great works (8:4-5), which is not where a man excluded for leprosy would normally be. Kings does not always arrange its material in order, and we are not told how to reconcile it. It is better to say so than to invent something.

Stand back at the end and look at the two servants this chapter has given us.

It opens with a girl who had been robbed of everything she had — her home, her family, her country and her freedom — standing in a foreign kitchen, and giving away the one thing she had left, which was what she knew about her God. She is not named and she never finds out what came of it.

It closes with a man who had everything she lacked — his own country, his liberty, his name in the record, and a place at the side of the greatest prophet of his generation — running down a road to turn it into silver.

She went home with nothing and he went home a leper, and the difference between them was not opportunity.

5.theology:
The LORD had given victory to Syria (v. 1). Dropped in as a subordinate clause: the God of Israel handing wins to Israel's enemy through a general who did not know his name — quite possibly including the raid that carried off the child who would tell that general where to be healed. He governs the armies of people who have never heard of him, and their spoils.

The address gets lost (vv. 3-7). A slave girl names the prophet in Samaria exactly. Kings turn it into diplomacy, and the king of Israel — who has a prophet a few streets away — tears his clothes and looks for the political trap. Chapter 1's question again: is there no God in Israel?

The script (v. 11). I thought that he would surely come out to me... He is not angry at being refused; he is being healed for nothing. He is angry at being healed the wrong way, without ceremony and without him. Most disappointment with God is of this kind — not that nothing came, but that it came through an ordinary person or a dull process instead of the way it had been staged in the mind.

Why the Jordan (v. 12). His objection is factually right: Abana and Pharpar are clear snow-melt and the lower Jordan is a brown ditch. Nothing in that river is good for skin. It is the border — the water Israel crossed to come in — and he is asked to go down into it seven times and come up unchanged six of them.

Carried by juniors (vv. 3, 13). A captive child tells him where to go and his own staff get him into the water, opening with my father and an argument he cannot answer. The great man is carried the whole distance by people whose names are not recorded.

Like the flesh of a little child (v. 14). Na'ar qaton — and the girl of verse 2 is na'arah qetannah, the same words in the feminine. His flesh came up like the flesh of the child who told him. The writer closes the circle in two words and says nothing about it.

Nazareth (Luke 4:27). There were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian. That, with the widow of Zarephath, was the sermon that made his home town try to throw him off a cliff.

Refused, so that it cannot be bought (v. 16). Elisha lives on gifts; he refuses this one because payment would turn the whole thing into a transaction between a rich foreigner and a useful holy man. Grace that can be paid for is not grace — and the question is reopened nine verses later by his own servant.

Rimmon (vv. 17-19). A four-minute-old believer with half-pagan theology (he wants Israelite soil for his altar) and an entirely real devotion (he will sacrifice to no other god). He raises the compromise himself, describes it three times in plain words, and asks pardon rather than permission. Elisha corrects neither his soil nor his conscience and says go in peace — a farewell, not a ruling. The compromise that troubles you is never the dangerous one; the dangerous one has gone quiet.

Was it a time? (v. 26). Elisha's list runs well past what was stolen — olive orchards, vineyards, sheep, oxen, servants — because he is naming the plan rather than the theft. And the charge is about timing: at the moment a Gentile was learning that God's mercy cannot be bought, the prophet's servant sold it to him. The leprosy did not vanish at the Jordan. It changed address.
5.examples:
Then: A girl who had been taken in a raid, stripped of her home, her family, her country, her freedom and even her name, stood in the kitchen of the man whose army did it and told his wife where he could be healed — and is never mentioned again, and so far as the record goes never found out what came of it.

Now: Three things. First, the script in verse 11. Take an honest inventory of your disappointment with God and see how much of it is that the answer came the wrong way — through somebody junior to you, or a long dull process, or a plain instruction with no ceremony attached. Naaman was being healed for free while he was raging. Second, Naaman's question about Rimmon. A man who names his one compromise out loud on the first day and asks God to pardon it is in a far better state than a long-standing believer who has stopped noticing his; the thing to fear is not the compromise that troubles you but the one that has gone silent. Third, the two servants. The chapter opens with someone who had nothing and gave away the best thing she knew, and closes with someone who had everything and sold it, and the difference between them was not opportunity.

And on the next day I said to her, 'Give your son, that we may eat him.' Now the king had dispatched a man from his presence, but before the messenger arrived Elisha said to the elders, "Do you see how this murderer has sent to take off my head? Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?"
6.overview:
Three scenes on wildly different scales, and the writer ties the first two together with a repeated cry. A student prophet loses a borrowed axe head in the Jordan and shouts alas, my master! Twenty verses later Elisha's servant walks out at dawn into a ring of Syrian chariots and shouts the same words. The panic is identical and so is the remedy.

At Dothan the answer is not reinforcement but sight. The hills were already full of horses and chariots of fire; nothing outside changed; Elisha prays open his eyes that he may see — which is the very condition his own inheritance turned on at the Jordan (2:10). The army is dazzled, walked into Samaria, and given a banquet by a king who wanted to kill them, and the raids stop.

Then the tone drops away entirely. Ben-hadad returns with his whole army, Samaria starves, and a woman on the wall brings the king a contract dispute about which of two mothers should have produced a child to be eaten. He tears his robes, the people see sackcloth against his skin, and his next sentence is an oath to behead the prophet. The chapter ends with a man announcing that he has finished waiting for God — one verse before the deliverance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Alas, My Master! It Was Borrowed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The company of prophets has outgrown its quarters and goes down to the Jordan to cut timber, with Elisha coming because they ask him to (vv. 1-4). A borrowed iron axe head flies off into the river, and the man's cry is alas, my master! It was borrowed (v. 5). Elisha asks where it fell, throws in a stick, and the iron floats; and the last word is not a presentation but an instruction — take it up (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Remember what Elijah believed about the size of this movement. I, even I only, am left, he said, twice, on Horeb (1 Kgs. 19:10, 14), and God answered with seven thousand. One generation later the problem is that the building is too small.
verseByVerse.examples: And this is the least consequential miracle in either book, done for the least consequential person in it. Nobody is healed and no army is turned; a poor student who was doing manual labour with a tool he could not afford to replace has lost it in the water, and the man who will stop an invasion eighteen verses later goes down to the river about it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the sons of the prophets said to Elisha, "See, the place where we dwell under your charge is too small for us. Let us go to the Jordan and each of us get there a log, and let us make a place for us to dwell there." And he answered, "Go." Then one of them said, "Be pleased to go with your servants." And he answered, "I will go." So he went with them. And when they came to the Jordan, they cut down trees. But as one was felling a log, his axe head fell into the water, and he cried out, "Alas, my master! It was borrowed." Then the man of God said, "Where did it fall?" When he showed him the place, he cut off a stick and threw it in there and made the iron float. And he said, "Take it up." So he reached out his hand and took it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the sons of the prophets said to Elisha, "See, the place where we dwell under your charge is too small for us.'

Before anything else, notice what kind of problem this is.

One generation ago a man sat under a bush in the desert and told God twice that he was the only one left, and meant it, and was answered with a number he had no way of checking — seven thousand knees that had not bowed (1 Kgs. 19:18). Now his successor is running a residential community of prophets that has outgrown its building.

Nobody ever gets to see that reversal happen in the middle of it. Elijah died believing the cause was down to one man. The overcrowding is his answer and he was not there for it.

'Let us go to the Jordan and each of us get there a log, and let us make a place for us to dwell there." And he answered, "Go."'

'Then one of them said, "Be pleased to go with your servants." And he answered, "I will go."'

They are cutting their own timber, because they have no money. And one of them asks the head of the school to come along — not to supervise, simply to be there — and he goes.

'So he went with them. And when they came to the Jordan, they cut down trees.'

'But as one was felling a log, his axe head fell into the water, and he cried out, "Alas, my master! It was borrowed."'

Take the size of this disaster properly, because it is easy to smile at and it was not funny to him.

Iron was expensive in that century. An axe head was a serious capital item, well beyond a student prophet living on donated barley, which is exactly why he did not own one. He had borrowed it, from somebody who trusted him with it, and it is now in the mud at the bottom of the Jordan.

He cannot replace it. He cannot pay for it. He has to go back to a neighbour and say so. It is the same shape as the widow's debt two chapters ago, in miniature: an obligation to a real person that he has no means of discharging.

Hold on to the words he shouts, because they will be shouted again in this chapter by somebody in an incomparably worse position. Alas, my master!

'Then the man of God said, "Where did it fall?" When he showed him the place, he cut off a stick and threw it in there and made the iron float.'

He asks where. The man points at a patch of moving brown water, and a stick goes in, and iron comes up.

A stick does not float iron, any more than salt sweetens a spring or flour draws poison out of a stew. The materials in Elisha's ministry are always chosen so that nobody can credit the material.

'And he said, "Take it up." So he reached out his hand and took it.'

Not here you are. Take it up. The man has to put his own hand into the river and close it round the thing he lost.

Now stand back and look at what this passage is doing in a chapter that also contains a besieging army, a blinded regiment and a woman who has eaten her child.

It is the smallest thing God does in either of these books, and it is done for the smallest person in them. No one is dying. No kingdom turns on it. A poor man doing manual labour has lost somebody else's tool and is embarrassed and frightened about it, and the prophet who will shortly stop a war walks down to the water's edge and deals with it.

There is a kind of piety that would be ashamed to trouble God with a lost axe head — that files its own small humiliations as beneath his notice and prays only about the large items. This chapter puts the axe head first, before the army, and gives it the same prophet.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–23 — Those Who Are With Us Are More
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elisha keeps telling Israel's king where the Syrian ambushes are laid, until Ben-hadad concludes he has a traitor — and is told the truth: the prophet in Israel tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom (v. 12). His response is to send an army by night to seize him at Dothan (vv. 13-14). Elisha's servant goes out at dawn, sees the ring of horses and chariots, and cries alas, my master! What shall we do? (v. 15). The answer is arithmetic that contradicts the evidence — those who are with us are more than those who are with them — and a prayer: O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see (vv. 16-17). The army is struck blind, led into Samaria, and given dinner (vv. 18-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing on those hills changed. The young man had been looking at them all morning and they were full of horses and chariots of fire the whole time. Elisha does not pray for reinforcements — the reinforcements are already there in overwhelming strength — he prays for eyes. And that is the very thing his own inheritance turned on: if you see me as I am being taken from you, it shall be so for you (2:10).
verseByVerse.examples: And the campaign ends with a banquet. He prepared for them a great feast, and when they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away... And the Syrians did not come again on raids into the land of Israel (v. 23). Proverbs said to do this and Paul quoted it — if your enemy is hungry, feed him (Prov. 25:21; Rom. 12:20). Here it is done, by a king who wanted to kill them, and it works.

verseByVerse.quote: Once when the king of Syria was warring against Israel, he took counsel with his servants, saying, "At such and such a place shall be my camp." But the man of God sent word to the king of Israel, "Beware that you do not pass this place, for the Syrians are going down there." And the king of Israel sent to the place about which the man of God told him. Thus he used to warn him, so that he saved himself there more than once or twice. And the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled because of this thing, and he called his servants and said to them, "Will you not show me who of us is for the king of Israel?" And one of his servants said, "None, my lord, O king; but Elisha, the prophet who is in Israel, tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom." And he said, "Go and see where he is, that I may send and seize him." It was told him, "Behold, he is in Dothan." So he sent there horses and chariots and a great army, and they came by night and surrounded the city. When the servant of the man of God rose early in the morning and went out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was all around the city. And the servant said, "Alas, my master! What shall we do?" He said, "Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them." Then Elisha prayed and said, "O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see." So the LORD opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha. And when the Syrians came down against him, Elisha prayed to the LORD and said, "Please strike this people with blindness." So he struck them with blindness in accordance with the prayer of Elisha. And Elisha said to them, "This is not the way, and this is not the city. Follow me, and I will bring you to the man whom you seek." And he led them to Samaria. As soon as they entered Samaria, Elisha said, "O LORD, open the eyes of these men, that they may see." So the LORD opened their eyes and they saw, and behold, they were in the midst of Samaria. As soon as the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha, "My father, shall I strike them down? Shall I strike them down?" He answered, "You shall not strike them down. Would you strike down those whom you have taken captive with your sword and with your bow? Set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink and go to their master." So he prepared for them a great feast, and when they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away, and they went to their master. And the Syrians did not come again on raids into the land of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Once when the king of Syria was warring against Israel, he took counsel with his servants, saying, "At such and such a place shall be my camp."'

'But the man of God sent word to the king of Israel, "Beware that you do not pass this place, for the Syrians are going down there."'

'And the king of Israel sent to the place about which the man of God told him. Thus he used to warn him, so that he saved himself there more than once or twice.'

Note the ordinariness of the arrangement. Thus he used to warn him — a standing practice, repeated often enough to be described as a habit.

Note who is being protected. This is Ahab's son, who keeps the calves, whose court prophets are his father's, and who will shortly swear to have Elisha's head off. God's prophet is running his intelligence service.

'And the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled because of this thing, and he called his servants and said to them, "Will you not show me who of us is for the king of Israel?"'

The natural conclusion. Repeated leaks means a traitor in the tent, and he goes looking for one.

'And one of his servants said, "None, my lord, O king; but Elisha, the prophet who is in Israel, tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom."'

Somebody on the Syrian staff has been keeping track of Israelite affairs, and he says a thing worth stopping over.

The words that you speak in your bedroom. Not the plans announced in council; the sentences said privately, at night, to nobody in particular, in the one room a king has to himself.

Take it out of the war for a moment. Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether (Ps. 139:4). What is said in the dark, in the last hour of the day, when the performance is over and there is nobody to impress — that is the material this verse is talking about, and it is not private.

That is a terror or a comfort depending on one thing only, which is whether the one listening is for you.

'And he said, "Go and see where he is, that I may send and seize him." It was told him, "Behold, he is in Dothan."'

He has just been informed that this man knows what he says in his bedroom, and his plan is a surprise raid.

The comedy and the theology are the same thing here. You cannot ambush a man who hears you planning the ambush. Ben-hadad is a competent soldier making a competent decision inside a world that does not exist, and everybody can see it except him.

'So he sent there horses and chariots and a great army, and they came by night and surrounded the city.'

Cavalry, chariots and a great army, moved at night, to take one unarmed man in a small town.

'When the servant of the man of God rose early in the morning and went out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was all around the city. And the servant said, "Alas, my master! What shall we do?"'

There is the cry again, word for word. Alas, my master!

A man said it twenty verses ago about a borrowed axe head in a river. A man says it now with a ring of Syrian chariots round the walls at first light. The writer has put the two cries in the same chapter on purpose, and the effect is to flatten the distance between them: the panic is identical, and so is the remedy.

Your small disasters and your large ones produce the same sentence out of you, and they are answered by the same person.

'He said, "Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them."'

This is arithmetic, and as arithmetic it is simply false. There are two of them in that house. There is an army outside. The servant can count and Elisha appears not to be able to.

'Then Elisha prayed and said, "O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see." So the LORD opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.'

Read the prayer carefully, because it is not the prayer we would have prayed.

He does not ask for deliverance. He does not ask God to send help, or to strike the enemy, or to open a way out. Help is already there, in overwhelming force, on the hillside the young man has been staring at since dawn.

What he asks for is eyes.

And nothing outside changed. That is the thing to hold. The horses of fire were on that mountain while the servant was walking out of the gate in a panic; they were there while he counted the Syrian chariots; they did not arrive in answer to the prayer. The only thing that altered in the whole valley was one young man's capacity to see what was in front of him.

That is exactly what Elisha's own inheritance turned on. If you see me as I am being taken from you, it shall be so for you (2:10). He was given eyes on the far side of the Jordan, and here he is spending them on somebody else's fear.

The fire imagery is not new either. Horses and chariots of fire came between him and Elijah in the whirlwind, and his cry then was my father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! (2:12). He said the country's real defence was a man with the word of God. Now his servant is allowed to look at it.

'And when the Syrians came down against him, Elisha prayed to the LORD and said, "Please strike this people with blindness." So he struck them with blindness in accordance with the prayer of Elisha.'

The word is a rare one, used elsewhere only of the men at Lot's door in Sodom (Gen. 19:11), and it seems to mean a dazzling or confusion rather than total darkness — these men can walk, follow a voice and cover the road to Samaria.

'And Elisha said to them, "This is not the way, and this is not the city. Follow me, and I will bring you to the man whom you seek." And he led them to Samaria.'

It is a ruse, and it should be called one rather than defended too eagerly or condemned too heavily. The text passes no judgement on it at all.

What can fairly be said is that the last clause is kept exactly. He does bring them to the man they are seeking. He walks in front of them the whole way and hands himself over in the middle of the enemy's capital, which is a strange thing for a deceiver to do.

'As soon as they entered Samaria, Elisha said, "O LORD, open the eyes of these men, that they may see." So the LORD opened their eyes and they saw, and behold, they were in the midst of Samaria.'

The same prayer as verse 17, for the other side. Twice in four verses he asks God to let men see what is actually around them, and both times it is a mercy, and both times it is terrifying to the man it happens to.

'As soon as the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha, "My father, shall I strike them down? Shall I strike them down?"'

He asks it twice, which tells you how much he wants to.

He calls the prophet my father, which is what Elisha called Elijah at the Jordan. It is an affectionate and deferential word, and the man who uses it here will be swearing to cut this father's head off before the chapter ends.

'He answered, "You shall not strike them down. Would you strike down those whom you have taken captive with your sword and with your bow? Set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink and go to their master."'

The argument is precise and it is about ownership. You did not take these men. Your bow did not bring one of them down; you were not there. They were handed to you, and a gift is not a trophy.

It is the same principle Elisha's master pressed on Ahab about Ben-hadad, and it cuts the opposite way here, which shows it was never a rule about sparing or killing. The question is always what God has appointed, and a man who has been given something has no right to treat it as something he won.

'So he prepared for them a great feast, and when they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away, and they went to their master. And the Syrians did not come again on raids into the land of Israel.'

He was told bread and water. He laid on a banquet.

Picture the scene, because it is one of the strangest in the Old Testament. A raiding force that marched all night to kidnap a prophet is sitting down in the enemy capital, at the enemy king's expense, eating a proper meal, and then walking home unharmed with a story to tell.

Proverbs had put it in writing: if your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink (Prov. 25:21), and Paul quotes exactly that when he tells Christians how to handle people who mean them harm (Rom. 12:20). The Lord said the same in four words: love your enemies (Matt. 5:44).

Here it is done, reluctantly, by a bad king under orders, and the result is in the last clause: the Syrians did not come again on raids into the land of Israel.

The most effective military operation in the book of Kings was a dinner.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–33 — A Woman on the Wall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ben-hadad comes back, not raiding but besieging, and Samaria starves until a donkey's head costs eighty shekels (vv. 24-25). A woman calls to the king from the wall, and her complaint is not the one he expects: she and a neighbour agreed to eat their sons in turn, so we boiled my son and ate him, and the other has hidden hers (vv. 28-29). The king tears his robes and the people see sackcloth against his skin (v. 30) — and his next sentence is an oath to have Elisha's head off before nightfall (v. 31). Elisha, sitting with the elders, knows the executioner is coming and knows the king is behind him (v. 32). And the chapter ends on the sentence of a man who has finished: this trouble is from the LORD! Why should I wait for the LORD any longer? (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: What is happening on that wall was written down centuries before as the specific sanction of a broken covenant: you shall eat the flesh of your sons (Lev. 26:29), and Deuteronomy spells it out at length for exactly this situation, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemy shall distress you (Deut. 28:53-57). This is not random horror. It is a clause coming due.
verseByVerse.examples: And notice what she is actually complaining about. Not the eating of a child — the breach of the agreement. The other woman has not kept her side. The moral sense is gone entirely and what is left standing in its place is contract law, and that is more frightening than the famine.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward Ben-hadad king of Syria mustered his entire army and went up and besieged Samaria. And there was a great famine in Samaria, as they besieged it, until a donkey's head was sold for eighty shekels of silver, and the fourth part of a kab of dove's dung for five shekels of silver. Now as the king of Israel was passing by on the wall, a woman cried out to him, saying, "Help, my lord, O king!" And he said, "If the LORD will not help you, how shall I help you? From the threshing floor, or from the winepress?" And the king asked her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "This woman said to me, 'Give your son, that we may eat him today, and we will eat my son tomorrow.' So we boiled my son and ate him. And on the next day I said to her, 'Give your son, that we may eat him.' But she has hidden her son." When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes—now he was passing by on the wall—and the people looked, and behold, he had sackcloth beneath on his body— and he said, "May God do so to me and more also, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat remains on his shoulders today." Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. Now the king had dispatched a man from his presence, but before the messenger arrived Elisha said to the elders, "Do you see how this murderer has sent to take off my head? Look, when the messenger comes, shut the door and hold the door fast against him. Is not the sound of his master's feet behind him?" And while he was still speaking with them, the messenger came down to him and said, "This trouble is from the LORD! Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Afterward Ben-hadad king of Syria mustered his entire army and went up and besieged Samaria.'

Do not read this as a contradiction of the verse before it. The raids stopped — the border skirmishing, the ambush parties, the seizing of prophets. What comes now is a different thing altogether: the entire army, in a formal siege, against the capital. Enemies are not always cured by kindness, and the Bible does not pretend otherwise.

'And there was a great famine in Samaria, as they besieged it, until a donkey's head was sold for eighty shekels of silver, and the fourth part of a kab of dove's dung for five shekels of silver.'

The prices are the report. A donkey is unclean and its head is the least edible part of it, and it is going for eighty shekels — years of a labourer's wages. The other item may be literally what it says, or it may be a country name for the bulbs of a wild plant; either way, half a pint of it costs five shekels.

People are paying fortunes for refuse. That is what a siege does, and the writer would rather show you a price list than describe it.

'Now as the king of Israel was passing by on the wall, a woman cried out to him, saying, "Help, my lord, O king!"'

'And he said, "If the LORD will not help you, how shall I help you? From the threshing floor, or from the winepress?"'

The answer is bitter and it is half right. There is no grain on the threshing floor and no wine in the press, and he cannot conjure either. What he cannot see is that his own sentence names the only person who could.

'And the king asked her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "This woman said to me, 'Give your son, that we may eat him today, and we will eat my son tomorrow.'

'So we boiled my son and ate him. And on the next day I said to her, 'Give your son, that we may eat him.' But she has hidden her son."'

Read it slowly. It will not be improved by hurrying.

Two mothers made an agreement. They ate one child on the first day. On the second day the other woman would not produce hers, and the first woman has come to the king of Israel for justice.

Now the thing that should stop you, which is not the cannibalism. It is what she is complaining about.

She is not asking for help, or for mercy, or for the war to end. She is bringing a contract dispute. She kept her side of the bargain and the other party has defaulted, and she wants the king to enforce it. There is not one word of horror in her mouth about what she did to her own son yesterday.

That is what starvation had done in Samaria, and it is a picture of what any sustained evil does to the people inside it. The moral sense goes first and the machinery of fairness keeps running, so that the last thing left standing in a person is a sense of grievance about being cheated.

All of this had been written down. Long before there was a Samaria to besiege, Moses had set out the sanctions of a broken covenant, and among them: you shall eat the flesh of your sons, and you shall eat the flesh of your daughters (Lev. 26:29). Deuteronomy goes further and describes it at appalling length, naming the siege and the distress with which your enemy shall distress you in all your towns, and the refined and gentle woman who will not share what she does in secret (Deut. 28:53-57).

This is not a random horror out of a brutal age. It is a clause coming due, in the exact circumstances the clause specified, in a kingdom that had spent a century and a half being warned.

'When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes—now he was passing by on the wall—and the people looked, and behold, he had sackcloth beneath on his body—'

The robes come apart and the people on the wall see what is underneath, and it is sackcloth, worn against the skin.

So he had been in mourning all along, privately, under his clothes, where nobody could see it. His father Ahab put sackcloth on his flesh too, when Elijah met him in Naboth's vineyard, and God noticed it and deferred a judgment for it (1 Kgs. 21:27-29).

Wait for the next verse before deciding what this one means.

'and he said, "May God do so to me and more also, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat remains on his shoulders today."'

There it is. Sackcloth against the skin, and an oath to behead the prophet, in consecutive sentences.

He is genuinely in anguish, and he is genuinely religious about it, and the direction of his fury is at the one man in Samaria who has been keeping him alive by telling him where the ambushes were. The sackcloth was real and it was not repentance. It was grief wearing the costume of repentance, with nothing underneath it that had changed.

That is a thing to test in yourself, and the test is not how bad you feel. It is what you do next with the person who has been telling you the truth.

'Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. Now the king had dispatched a man from his presence, but before the messenger arrived Elisha said to the elders, "Do you see how this murderer has sent to take off my head? Look, when the messenger comes, shut the door and hold the door fast against him. Is not the sound of his master's feet behind him?"'

He knows before the man is at the door, as he knew what was said in a Syrian bedroom.

This murderer — the Hebrew is literally this son of a murderer, and the reader is meant to supply the father's name. Naboth is still on the account; the vineyard is one chapter back in the reader's memory and thirteen years back in the kingdom's.

The last question is the shrewd one: is not the sound of his master's feet behind him? The king sent an executioner and then came after him. Whatever he means to do at that door, he has not been able to stay away from it.

'And while he was still speaking with them, the messenger came down to him and said, "This trouble is from the LORD! Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?"'

That is where the chapter stops.

Whoever says it — the messenger, or the king a step behind him — it is the most honest sentence anybody speaks in these two chapters, and it is a surrender. He has got two things right: the trouble is from the LORD, and waiting is what has been asked of him. And he has finished. He is not denying that God is there. He is announcing that he has come to the end of what he can bear of waiting for him.

Anyone who has prayed a long time about something that is getting worse knows the sentence. It is not usually spoken in a fit of unbelief. It is spoken flatly, by an exhausted person, as a conclusion.

Now notice where the writer has put it. It is the last verse of the chapter, and the words that follow it, in the very next breath, are: hear the word of the LORD... tomorrow about this time.

He gave up one sentence early.

6.theology:
Too small for us (v. 1). Elijah said twice on Horeb that he was the only one left and was answered with seven thousand (1 Kgs. 19:18). A generation later the problem is that the building will not hold the students. He never saw it. Nobody is shown the reversal while they are standing in the middle of it.

The axe head (vv. 5-7). The smallest thing God does in either book, done for the smallest person in them, and placed first — before the army. A poor man has lost a borrowed tool he cannot replace and is frightened about facing the neighbour who lent it. There is a piety that would be ashamed to trouble God with that; this chapter gives it the same prophet as the invasion.

The words you speak in your bedroom (v. 12). Not the council chamber — the room a king has to himself, at night, with the performance over. Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether (Ps. 139:4). Whether that is terror or comfort depends on exactly one thing: whether the one listening is for you. And Ben-hadad, told this, responds by planning a surprise raid — which is the comedy and the theology in one stroke.

He prays for eyes, not for help (v. 17). The horses of fire were on that mountain the whole time the servant was counting Syrian chariots. Nothing in the valley changed except one young man's capacity to see what was already in front of him. And sight is precisely what Elisha's own inheritance was made conditional on (2:10) — the gift he was given is the gift he spends on somebody else's fear.

Those whom you have taken captive (v. 22). The argument is about ownership: your bow did not bring one of them down, so they are not your trophies but a gift, and a gift may not be treated as a conquest. And what follows is the most effective military operation in the book — if your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat (Prov. 25:21; Rom. 12:20), done grudgingly by a bad king, after which the raids stop. Verse 24 is a siege, not a raid; kindness is not a guarantee against every future enemy, and Scripture does not claim it is.

The clause coming due (vv. 28-29). Cannibalism in a besieged city is named in the covenant sanctions in advance — you shall eat the flesh of your sons (Lev. 26:29), set out at appalling length in Deut. 28:53-57 for exactly these circumstances. And the horror inside it is that the woman is not appalled: she brings a breach-of-contract case. Sustained evil takes the moral sense first and leaves the machinery of fairness running, so that the last thing alive in a person is a grievance about being cheated.

Sackcloth where it does not show (vv. 30-31). He had been wearing it against his skin under the robes, as his father Ahab did (1 Kgs. 21:27) — and his next sentence is an oath to take the prophet's head. The grief was real; it was not repentance. The test of that is never how bad a man feels, but what he does next with the person who has been telling him the truth.

One verse early (v. 33). Why should I wait for the LORD any longer? is not a denial that God is there — it grants that the trouble is from him and that waiting was the thing asked. It is an exhausted man announcing a conclusion. The next words on the page are hear the word of the LORD... tomorrow about this time.
6.examples:
Then: A young man walked out of a gate at first light to start the day, found the hills solid with the chariots of an army that had marched all night to take his master, and cried out in exactly the words another man had used about an axe head at the bottom of a river.

Now: Three things. First, the axe head is placed before the army on purpose. If you have a category of trouble too small to pray about — the embarrassment, the thing you have broken that belongs to someone else, the sum you cannot quite cover — this chapter puts it first and gives it the same prophet as the invasion. Second, the prayer at Dothan is not for rescue but for eyes, and nothing outside changed when it was answered. Before asking God to alter your circumstances, ask him to show you what is already standing in them. Third, verse 33. Almost nobody gives up on God in a fit of unbelief; they give up flatly, exhausted, as a reasonable conclusion, having waited a long time while things got worse. That sentence is the last in the chapter, and the first words of the next one are tomorrow about this time.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>But Elisha said, "Hear the word of the LORD: thus says the LORD, Tomorrow about this time a seah of fine flour shall be sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, at the gate of Samaria."<sup>2</sup>Then the captain on whose hand the king leaned said to the man of God, "If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could this thing be?" But he said, "You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it."<sup>3</sup>Now there were four men who were lepers at the entrance to the gate. And they said to one another, "Why are we sitting here until we die?<sup>4</sup>If we say, 'Let us enter the city,' the famine is in the city, and we shall die there. And if we sit here, we die also. So now come, let us go over to the camp of the Syrians. If they spare our lives we shall live, and if they kill us we shall but die."<sup>5</sup>So they arose at twilight to go to the camp of the Syrians. But when they came to the edge of the camp of the Syrians, behold, there was no one there.<sup>6</sup>For the Lord had made the army of the Syrians hear the sound of chariots and of horses, the sound of a great army, so that they said to one another, "Behold, the king of Israel has hired against us the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to come against us."<sup>7</sup>So they fled away in the twilight and abandoned their tents, their horses, and their donkeys, leaving the camp as it was, and fled for their lives.<sup>8</sup>And when these lepers came to the edge of the camp, they went into a tent and ate and drank, and they carried off silver and gold and clothing and went and hid them. Then they came back and entered another tent and carried off things from it and went and hid them.<sup>9</sup>Then they said to one another, "We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news. If we are silent and wait until the morning light, punishment will overtake us. Now therefore come; let us go and tell the king's household."<sup>10</sup>So they came and called to the gatekeepers of the city and told them, "We came to the camp of the Syrians, and behold, there was no one to be seen or heard there, nothing but the horses tied and the donkeys tied and the tents as they were."<sup>11</sup>Then the gatekeepers called out, and it was told within the king's household.<sup>12</sup>And the king rose in the night and said to his servants, "I will tell you what the Syrians have done to us. They know that we are hungry. Therefore they have gone out of the camp to hide themselves in the open country, thinking, 'When they come out of the city, we shall take them alive and get into the city.'"<sup>13</sup>And one of his servants said, "Let some men take five of the remaining horses, seeing that those who are left here will fare like the whole multitude of Israel who have already perished. Let us send and see."<sup>14</sup>So they took two horsemen, and the king sent them after the army of the Syrians, saying, "Go and see."<sup>15</sup>So they went after them as far as the Jordan, and behold, all the way was littered with garments and equipment that the Syrians had thrown away in their haste. And the messengers returned and told the king.<sup>16</sup>Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Syrians. So a seah of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD.<sup>17</sup>Now the king had appointed the captain on whose hand he leaned to have charge of the gate. And the people trampled him in the gate, so that he died, as the man of God had said when the king came down to him.<sup>18</sup>For when the man of God had said to the king, "Two seahs of barley shall be sold for a shekel, and a seah of fine flour for a shekel, about this time tomorrow in the gate of Samaria,"<sup>19</sup>the captain had answered the man of God, "If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could such a thing be?" And he had said, "You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it."<sup>20</sup>And so it happened to him, for the people trampled him in the gate and he died.
7.overview:
Chapter 6 ended with a man announcing that he had finished waiting for God. Chapter 7 begins in the next breath with a price list: flour and barley, at named rates, at the gate of Samaria, tomorrow. It is a promise built to be checked, and the rates are not miraculous rates — they are what food costs in an ordinary year. What is being promised to a city where women are eating their children is that by this time tomorrow people will be able to do the shopping.

The king's closest aide sneers at it and is told he will see it and not taste it. And then the deliverance is found by the four people in the district with nothing left to lose: lepers sitting outside the gate because the law put them there, who reason that surrender might kill them and staying certainly will. They walk into an abandoned camp — an entire army has fled from the sound of chariots that did not exist — and eat, and loot two tents, and then stop: we are not doing right. This day is a day of good news.

Inside the walls the king explains the good news away as an ambush; a servant with no rank talks him into checking; the road to the Jordan is littered with thrown-away kit for twenty-five miles; and the flour sells at the price that was named. The officer who sneered is posted to the gate, and is trampled there.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against a king who has just announced that he is finished waiting, Elisha puts a price list: tomorrow about this time a seah of fine flour shall be sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, at the gate of Samaria (v. 1).
