The officer the king leans on answers with a sneer — if the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could this thing be? — and is told exactly what will happen to him: you shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: Notice how falsifiable the promise is. Not God will provide, but a time, a place, two commodities and an exchange rate, given to a city where a donkey's head costs eighty shekels. Twenty-four hours, at a named gate, checkable by anybody with a purse.
verseByVerse.examples: And the rates quoted are not miraculous rates. They are ordinary market prices — what flour and barley cost in a normal year. The wonder being promised is not abundance. It is that by this time tomorrow a starving city will be able to do its shopping.

verseByVerse.quote: But Elisha said, "Hear the word of the LORD: thus says the LORD, Tomorrow about this time a seah of fine flour shall be sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, at the gate of Samaria." Then the captain on whose hand the king leaned said to the man of God, "If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could this thing be?" But he said, "You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But Elisha said, "Hear the word of the LORD: thus says the LORD, Tomorrow about this time a seah of fine flour shall be sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, at the gate of Samaria."'

The last words of the previous chapter were a man saying he had finished waiting for God. These are the next words on the page.

Look at the form the answer takes, because it is not the form comfort usually takes.

He does not say that God is good, or that the siege will lift, or that help is coming. He gives a time — tomorrow, about this hour. A place — the gate of Samaria. Two commodities, fine flour and barley. And an exchange rate for each.

That is a promise made deliberately checkable. Anybody in the city with a shekel and a twenty-four-hour memory can hold it up against the facts, and if it fails Elisha is finished.

Then notice what the rates actually are. A seah of flour for a shekel is not a giveaway; it is roughly what flour cost in an ordinary year. He is not promising a windfall or a feast. He is promising that by this time tomorrow, in a city where a donkey's head is going for eighty shekels and women are eating their children, people will be able to do the shopping at normal prices.

Sometimes the thing God promises is not abundance. It is Tuesday, back the way it should have been.

'Then the captain on whose hand the king leaned said to the man of God, "If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could this thing be?" But he said, "You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it."'

The man is the king's aide — literally the officer on whose hand the king leans, which is the identical expression used of Naaman's duty in the temple of Rimmon two chapters ago. He is the closest man to the throne, and the first to speak.

His sneer is well constructed, and it is built out of Scripture. Windows in heaven is flood language: at the deluge the windows of the heavens were opened (Gen. 7:11). It is also blessing language, and Malachi will use it for the most extravagant promise in the prophets — put me to the test, says the LORD, and see if I will not open the windows of heaven for you (Mal. 3:10).

So what he is saying is: even if God did the biggest thing anybody has ever heard of, this could not happen. He is not denying that God exists or that God is powerful. He is denying that a particular word, just spoken in his hearing, could possibly be true.

Be careful with the reply, because it is not a curse thrown at a heckler. It is a sentence measured to the offence. You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it. The man who said the promise could not be kept will be given the fullest possible proof that it was, and no share in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–11 — This Day Is a Day of Good News
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four lepers sitting outside the gate, where the law required them to be, work out that they will die in the city, die where they are, or possibly live if they surrender — if they kill us we shall but die (vv. 3-4). They walk into an empty camp: the Lord had made the army of the Syrians hear the sound of chariots and of horses, the sound of a great army, and it had run in the dusk leaving everything standing (vv. 5-7). They eat, drink and loot two tents — and then stop. We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news. If we are silent and wait until the morning light, punishment will overtake us (v. 9). So they go back and shout it to the gatekeepers (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The men the law had put outside the community are the ones who find the deliverance of the community, and they go because they are the only people in the district with nothing left to lose. Everyone inside the wall still had something to protect, and nobody inside the wall went out to look.
verseByVerse.examples: And the phrase in verse 9 is besorah — the Hebrew word that stands behind the New Testament's euangelion, good news, gospel. Four starving outcasts who have found more food than they can carry decide that eating it quietly while the city dies is not a thing they can do. That is the church, described eight centuries early, down to the mixed motives.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were four men who were lepers at the entrance to the gate. And they said to one another, "Why are we sitting here until we die? If we say, 'Let us enter the city,' the famine is in the city, and we shall die there. And if we sit here, we die also. So now come, let us go over to the camp of the Syrians. If they spare our lives we shall live, and if they kill us we shall but die." So they arose at twilight to go to the camp of the Syrians. But when they came to the edge of the camp of the Syrians, behold, there was no one there. For the Lord had made the army of the Syrians hear the sound of chariots and of horses, the sound of a great army, so that they said to one another, "Behold, the king of Israel has hired against us the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to come against us." So they fled away in the twilight and abandoned their tents, their horses, and their donkeys, leaving the camp as it was, and fled for their lives. And when these lepers came to the edge of the camp, they went into a tent and ate and drank, and they carried off silver and gold and clothing and went and hid them. Then they came back and entered another tent and carried off things from it and went and hid them. Then they said to one another, "We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news. If we are silent and wait until the morning light, punishment will overtake us. Now therefore come; let us go and tell the king's household." So they came and called to the gatekeepers of the city and told them, "We came to the camp of the Syrians, and behold, there was no one to be seen or heard there, nothing but the horses tied and the donkeys tied and the tents as they were." Then the gatekeepers called out, and it was told within the king's household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now there were four men who were lepers at the entrance to the gate. And they said to one another, "Why are we sitting here until we die?'

They are at the gate because that is where the law put them. A man with that condition shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp (Lev. 13:46). In a walled city under siege, outside the camp means the strip of ground between the gate and the enemy, which is the worst real estate in the world.

They are excluded, starving, and closer to the Syrian lines than anybody else in Israel.

'If we say, 'Let us enter the city,' the famine is in the city, and we shall die there. And if we sit here, we die also. So now come, let us go over to the camp of the Syrians. If they spare our lives we shall live, and if they kill us we shall but die."'

It is a piece of clear-eyed arithmetic done by men with nothing.

Three options, and two of them are certain death. The third might be death and might not. If they kill us we shall but die — that is the whole calculation, and there is not a scrap of heroism in it. They are not brave. They have simply run out of things that could be taken from them.

That is exactly why it is these four who go. Everybody behind that wall still had something to protect — a house, a position, a last handful of grain, a reason to sit tight one more night. Nobody inside the city walked out to look. The men with nothing left to lose are the ones who find out that the siege is over.

'So they arose at twilight to go to the camp of the Syrians. But when they came to the edge of the camp of the Syrians, behold, there was no one there.'

'For the Lord had made the army of the Syrians hear the sound of chariots and of horses, the sound of a great army, so that they said to one another, "Behold, the king of Israel has hired against us the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to come against us."'

A small thing in the printing, first. Your Bible prints Lord here in ordinary letters rather than the small capitals it uses for the covenant name, because the Hebrew word is adonai, the Master. It happens exactly twice in this book. Do not build much on it — but the title chosen at this moment is the one that means sovereign ownership, and what is being described is God moving an entire army off a battlefield with a noise.

Now count the chariots in these two chapters, because there are three sets of them and only one is made of anything.

In chapter 6 a servant walked out at dawn into a ring of real Syrian chariots and panicked. On the same hillside, invisible to him, stood horses and chariots of fire, and he was terrified beside them until his eyes were opened. And here an entire professional army hears chariots that do not exist at all, and runs.

The Syrians were routed by a sound. Nobody drew a sword. God gave them the noise of the very thing they were most afraid of, and their own imaginations did the rest — they even supply the explanation themselves, complete with a list of the mercenary powers they assume have been hired against them.

'So they fled away in the twilight and abandoned their tents, their horses, and their donkeys, leaving the camp as it was, and fled for their lives.'

Everything left standing. Tents up, animals tethered, food on the fires. They did not strike camp; they ran out of it.

'And when these lepers came to the edge of the camp, they went into a tent and ate and drank, and they carried off silver and gold and clothing and went and hid them. Then they came back and entered another tent and carried off things from it and went and hid them.'

They do the entirely human thing first.

Four men who have been starving outside a gate walk into a tent with food in it, and they eat, and then they start burying treasure. A second tent, and more of it. Nobody should be surprised, and the writer does not scold them for it.

'Then they said to one another, "We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news. If we are silent and wait until the morning light, punishment will overtake us. Now therefore come; let us go and tell the king's household."'

Somewhere between the second tent and the third, one of them says it, and this is one of the great verses of the Old Testament.

We are not doing right.

Nothing had changed outside them. The camp was still empty and the silver was still theirs for the taking and nobody in Samaria knew anything about it. What happened was that four men, in the middle of the best night of their lives, could not go on enjoying it.

Be honest about the order of their reasons, because the text is. It is conscience first — we are not doing right. Then fear — punishment will overtake us, and they are correct, since a city that discovered they had sat on this would not have been gentle. Compassion for the starving is not actually mentioned.

Take the comfort in that. Their motives were a mixture, and God used them anyway, and the news got told. Nobody has to wait for a pure heart before opening their mouth.

Then the phrase itself: this day is a day of good news. The Hebrew is besorah, and it is the word that stands behind the Greek euangelion — good news, gospel. The Old Testament's clearest picture of evangelism is four ceremonially unclean men, excluded by law from the congregation, who have found more bread than they can eat while the city that shut them out is starving, and who decide at two in the morning that they cannot keep it to themselves.

That is the shape of the thing exactly. Not experts with a strategy — beggars who found food, going back to tell other beggars where it is.

'So they came and called to the gatekeepers of the city and told them, "We came to the camp of the Syrians, and behold, there was no one to be seen or heard there, nothing but the horses tied and the donkeys tied and the tents as they were."'

'Then the gatekeepers called out, and it was told within the king's household.'

They shout it up to men who are not allowed to let them in, and the gatekeepers pass it straight on without hesitating. The message runs up the chain in two verses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–20 — You Shall See It With Your Own Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king cannot believe it and constructs a theory of an ambush; a servant points out that the horses they would risk are dying anyway, and two are sent to look (vv. 12-14). The road to the Jordan is littered with garments and equipment that the Syrians had thrown away in their haste (v. 15). The people go out and plunder the camp, so a seah of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD (v. 16). And the officer who sneered, having been put in charge of the gate, is trampled there and dies — with the writer repeating the whole exchange so that nobody can miss it (vv. 17-20).
verseByVerse.theology: Everyone in this chapter is slow except the four men who had nothing. The lepers hesitate for the length of two tents; the gatekeepers pass it on at once; and the king, given verified good news in the middle of the night, sits up in bed and works out how it might be a trap.
verseByVerse.examples: And the sentence on the captain is exact rather than merely severe. He was not condemned for doubting that God can do things; he sneered at a particular word that had just been spoken in his hearing. He was told he would see it and not eat of it, he was posted to the very gate the prophecy had named, and he watched the price of flour come true over the top of him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king rose in the night and said to his servants, "I will tell you what the Syrians have done to us. They know that we are hungry. Therefore they have gone out of the camp to hide themselves in the open country, thinking, 'When they come out of the city, we shall take them alive and get into the city.'" And one of his servants said, "Let some men take five of the remaining horses, seeing that those who are left here will fare like the whole multitude of Israel who have already perished. Let us send and see." So they took two horsemen, and the king sent them after the army of the Syrians, saying, "Go and see." So they went after them as far as the Jordan, and behold, all the way was littered with garments and equipment that the Syrians had thrown away in their haste. And the messengers returned and told the king. Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Syrians. So a seah of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD. Now the king had appointed the captain on whose hand he leaned to have charge of the gate. And the people trampled him in the gate, so that he died, as the man of God had said when the king came down to him. For when the man of God had said to the king, "Two seahs of barley shall be sold for a shekel, and a seah of fine flour for a shekel, about this time tomorrow in the gate of Samaria," the captain had answered the man of God, "If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could such a thing be?" And he had said, "You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it." And so it happened to him, for the people trampled him in the gate and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the king rose in the night and said to his servants, "I will tell you what the Syrians have done to us. They know that we are hungry. Therefore they have gone out of the camp to hide themselves in the open country, thinking, 'When they come out of the city, we shall take them alive and get into the city.'"'

He is given the best news in a generation and immediately explains it away.

The theory is not stupid — feigned retreat was a standard tactic and he is a soldier. But look at the sequence of the man. Yesterday he swore to behead the prophet; last night he announced that he had finished waiting for God; and now, handed the fulfilment before breakfast, he sits up in the dark and works out how it must be a trap.

A settled expectation of the worst does not lift when the good arrives. It simply goes to work on the good.

'And one of his servants said, "Let some men take five of the remaining horses, seeing that those who are left here will fare like the whole multitude of Israel who have already perished. Let us send and see."'

Another servant, and again it is a servant, talks sense to a king. The argument is as bleak as the lepers' was: these horses are going to die with the rest of us, so there is nothing to lose by risking them.

Twice in two chapters the useful sentence comes from somebody with no rank at all.

'So they took two horsemen, and the king sent them after the army of the Syrians, saying, "Go and see."'

'So they went after them as far as the Jordan, and behold, all the way was littered with garments and equipment that the Syrians had thrown away in their haste. And the messengers returned and told the king.'

Twenty-five miles of dropped kit.

Men throw away armour and cloaks when they believe something is directly behind them, and the road to the Jordan is a record of a terror that had no cause. It is the most complete rout in the book and nobody in Israel was present for any of it.

'Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Syrians. So a seah of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD.'

The verse repeats the prophecy word for word as a price report. Same commodities, same rates, same gate, one day later.

'Now the king had appointed the captain on whose hand he leaned to have charge of the gate. And the people trampled him in the gate, so that he died, as the man of God had said when the king came down to him.'

Of all the postings in the city, he is given the gate.

Whatever the king intended by it — crowd control, most likely, at the one place everything was about to come through — the effect is that the man who said the thing could not happen is standing at the exact spot where it happens, holding back a starving population that has just been told there is food outside.

He saw it with his own eyes. He did not eat of it.

'For when the man of God had said to the king, "Two seahs of barley shall be sold for a shekel, and a seah of fine flour for a shekel, about this time tomorrow in the gate of Samaria,"'

'the captain had answered the man of God, "If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could such a thing be?" And he had said, "You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it."'

'And so it happened to him, for the people trampled him in the gate and he died.'

The writer sets the whole exchange out a second time, question and answer, and then states the outcome again in one line. He has told us this twice in four verses because he does not intend a single reader to reach the end of the chapter thinking it was a coincidence.

Be exact about what the man died for, because it is easy to make him a warning about doubt in general and he is not that. He was not executed for finding a promise hard to believe; half the people in this book find promises hard to believe, and Elisha's own servant panicked at Dothan without being trampled. He stood next to a prophet who had just spoken a specific word from God, and sneered at it.

There is a mercy folded into even that sentence, though it is a hard one. He was told in advance, in plain words, what would happen, and he had a day.

Set the two ends of the chapter beside each other and leave them there. It opened with the man closest to the throne, inside the walls, who heard the promise first and treated it as absurd. It ran through four men the law had put outside the gate, who had no standing, no health and no prospects, and who found the deliverance and could not keep quiet about it.

The city was saved by the people it had excluded, and the news reached the palace because four starving men decided at two in the morning that a day of good news is not a thing you eat by yourself.

7.theology:
The shape of the promise (v. 1). Not God is good but a time, a place, two commodities and an exchange rate — deliberately falsifiable, checkable by anyone with a shekel and a day's memory. And the rates are ordinary. Sometimes what God promises is not abundance but Tuesday, back the way it should have been.

Windows in heaven (v. 2). The sneer is built out of Scripture — the phrase is the flood's (Gen. 7:11) and Malachi's greatest promise (Mal. 3:10). He is not denying God's power in the abstract; he is denying that this particular word, spoken in his hearing a moment ago, could be true. That is what he dies for, and the sentence is measured to it exactly: the fullest possible proof, and no share.

Outside the camp (vv. 3-4). The law put them there (Lev. 13:46), and they are the ones who find the deliverance of the city that excluded them — because they are the only people in the district with nothing left to protect. Nobody inside the wall went out to look.

Three sets of chariots. Real Syrian ones that terrified a servant (6:15); fiery ones standing on the same hill that he could not see (6:17); and these, which do not exist at all (7:6). An army is routed by a noise, supplies its own explanation, and throws its equipment away for twenty-five miles. Nobody in Israel drew a sword.

A day of good news (v. 9). Besorah — the word behind euangelion. The Old Testament's clearest picture of evangelism is four unclean men, excluded by law, who found more bread than they could eat while the city that shut them out was starving, and could not go on eating it quietly. Beggars telling beggars where the food is. And the order of their reasons is honest — conscience first, then fear of what will happen when it comes out; compassion is not mentioned. God used the mixture, and the news got told. Nobody has to wait for a pure heart before opening their mouth.

Explaining the good away (v. 12). Handed the fulfilment in the middle of the night, the king sits up and reasons out how it must be a trap. A settled expectation of the worst does not lift when good news arrives; it goes to work on the good news.

Told twice (vv. 17-20). The writer repeats the whole exchange and then restates the outcome, because he does not intend one reader to finish the chapter thinking it a coincidence. And the man was not condemned for finding a promise hard — Elisha's own servant panicked at Dothan and was given eyes. He sneered at a word he had just heard God speak, and he was told a day in advance exactly what it would cost.
7.examples:
Then: Four men who were not allowed inside the gate sat in the strip of ground between a starving city and a besieging army, worked out that every option except one ended in certain death, and walked toward the enemy at dusk because they had nothing left that anybody could take.

Now: Three things. First, verse 9 is the missionary verse of the Old Testament, and what makes it usable is how unflattering it is. They had already eaten and buried treasure in two tents before conscience caught up with them, and their stated reasons were that it was wrong and that they would be punished — not that they felt for the starving. Mixed motives did not disqualify them and will not disqualify you. Second, the king in the night. If you have prayed a long time for something and are braced for disappointment, notice how easily a man in this chapter converts an answer into evidence of a trap; a habit of expecting the worst does not switch off when the good arrives. Third, who found it. The people with the least to protect went and looked, and everyone with something to lose stayed behind the wall and starved a little longer.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Elisha had said to the woman whose son he had restored to life, "Arise, and depart with your household, and sojourn wherever you can, for the LORD has called for a famine, and it will come upon the land for seven years."<sup>2</sup>So the woman arose and did according to the word of the man of God. She went with her household and sojourned in the land of the Philistines seven years.<sup>3</sup>And at the end of the seven years, when the woman returned from the land of the Philistines, she went to appeal to the king for her house and her land.<sup>4</sup>Now the king was talking with Gehazi the servant of the man of God, saying, "Tell me all the great things that Elisha has done."<sup>5</sup>And while he was telling the king how Elisha had restored the dead to life, behold, the woman whose son he had restored to life appealed to the king for her house and her land. And Gehazi said, "My lord, O king, here is the woman, and here is her son whom Elisha restored to life."<sup>6</sup>And when the king asked the woman, she told him. So the king appointed an official for her, saying, "Restore all that was hers, together with all the produce of the fields from the day that she left the land until now."<sup>7</sup>Now Elisha came to Damascus. Ben-hadad the king of Syria was sick. And when it was told him, "The man of God has come here,"<sup>8</sup>the king said to Hazael, "Take a present with you and go to meet the man of God, and inquire of the LORD through him, saying, 'Shall I recover from this sickness?'"<sup>9</sup>So Hazael went to meet him, and took a present with him, all kinds of goods of Damascus, forty camels' loads. When he came and stood before him, he said, "Your son Ben-hadad king of Syria has sent me to you, saying, 'Shall I recover from this sickness?'"<sup>10</sup>And Elisha said to him, "Go, say to him, 'You shall certainly recover,' but the LORD has shown me that he shall certainly die."<sup>11</sup>And he fixed his gaze and stared at him, until he was embarrassed. And the man of God wept.<sup>12</sup>And Hazael said, "Why does my lord weep?" He answered, "Because I know the evil that you will do to the people of Israel. You will set on fire their fortresses, and you will kill their young men with the sword and dash in pieces their little ones and rip open their pregnant women."<sup>13</sup>And Hazael said, "What is your servant, who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing?" Elisha answered, "The LORD has shown me that you are to be king over Syria."<sup>14</sup>Then he departed from Elisha and came to his master, who said to him, "What did Elisha say to you?" And he answered, "He told me that you would certainly recover."<sup>15</sup>But the next day he took the bed cloth and dipped it in water and spread it over his face, till he died. And Hazael became king in his place.<sup>16</sup>In the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab, king of Israel, when Jehoshaphat was king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, began to reign.<sup>17</sup>He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.<sup>18</sup>And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.<sup>19</sup>Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.<sup>20</sup>In his days Edom revolted from the rule of Judah and set up a king of their own.<sup>21</sup>Then Joram passed over to Zair with all his chariots and rose by night, and he and his chariot commanders struck the Edomites who had surrounded him, but his army fled home.<sup>22</sup>So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time.<sup>23</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Joram, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>24</sup>So Joram slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.<sup>25</sup>In the twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab, king of Israel, Ahaziah the son of Jehoram, king of Judah, began to reign.<sup>26</sup>Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah; she was a granddaughter of Omri king of Israel.<sup>27</sup>He also walked in the way of the house of Ahab and did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done, for he was son-in-law to the house of Ahab.<sup>28</sup>He went with Joram the son of Ahab to make war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead, and the Syrians wounded Joram.<sup>29</sup>And King Joram returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that the Syrians had given him at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was sick.
8.overview:
Three scenes, and the third one loads the gun for chapter 9.

The woman of Shunem, warned of a seven-year famine, comes home to find her land gone and walks into the palace to appeal — at the precise moment Gehazi is telling the king how Elisha raised a dead boy. She had refused an introduction to the king years earlier (I dwell among my own people, 4:13); God provides a better one than the one she declined, and she gets her land back with seven years of harvests added.

Then Damascus, where Elisha stares at a Syrian officer until the man squirms, and then weeps — because he has been shown the atrocities Hazael will commit. What is your servant, who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing? asks Hazael, and smothers his master the next morning, completing an instruction God gave Elijah on Horeb a generation before.

And then Judah, where the writer states the cause in the same breath as the verdict: the king behaved like the house of Ahab for the daughter of Ahab was his wife. Only the lamp promised to David keeps the kingdom standing. The chapter ends with both kings gathered at Jezreel — Naboth's town, where a sentence has been waiting thirteen years.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Here Is the Woman, and Here Is Her Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elisha had warned the woman of Shunem of a seven-year famine and told her to go; she spent the seven years in Philistine country and came back to find her house and land gone (vv. 1-3). She arrives at the palace to appeal — and the king happens at that moment to be asking Gehazi to tell me all the great things that Elisha has done. And while he was telling the king how Elisha had restored the dead to life, she walks in with the boy (vv. 4-5). Everything is restored, with the income of seven years' harvests added (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Go back to chapter 4 and remember what she turned down. Offered a word spoken on your behalf to the king or to the commander of the army, she answered I dwell among my own people (4:13) — no patron, no favours, nothing owed. Years later she needs precisely that introduction, and God arranges a better one than the one she declined: she does not have to make her case at all, because a servant is already telling her story to the king when she opens the door.
verseByVerse.examples: And Gehazi's presence at court is a difficulty worth naming rather than smoothing over. He was made a leper in chapter 5, and lepers did not chat with kings. Verse 1 has already signalled that we are in a flashback — Elisha had said — and Kings does not always lay its material out in order. It is better to say that than to invent a reconciliation the text does not offer.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Elisha had said to the woman whose son he had restored to life, "Arise, and depart with your household, and sojourn wherever you can, for the LORD has called for a famine, and it will come upon the land for seven years." So the woman arose and did according to the word of the man of God. She went with her household and sojourned in the land of the Philistines seven years. And at the end of the seven years, when the woman returned from the land of the Philistines, she went to appeal to the king for her house and her land. Now the king was talking with Gehazi the servant of the man of God, saying, "Tell me all the great things that Elisha has done." And while he was telling the king how Elisha had restored the dead to life, behold, the woman whose son he had restored to life appealed to the king for her house and her land. And Gehazi said, "My lord, O king, here is the woman, and here is her son whom Elisha restored to life." And when the king asked the woman, she told him. So the king appointed an official for her, saying, "Restore all that was hers, together with all the produce of the fields from the day that she left the land until now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Elisha had said to the woman whose son he had restored to life, "Arise, and depart with your household, and sojourn wherever you can, for the LORD has called for a famine, and it will come upon the land for seven years."'

Had said. The writer is reaching back; this is not the next thing that happened after the siege lifted, and Kings is not always laid out in the order events occurred.

Note the phrase the LORD has called for a famine. Called for it, as a man calls a servant. Seven years of failed harvests across a whole region are not weather; they are summoned.

She is given a warning and a lead time. She is not spared the famine — she has to leave her home for seven years — but she is told, and being told is itself a mercy the rest of the country does not get.

'So the woman arose and did according to the word of the man of God. She went with her household and sojourned in the land of the Philistines seven years.'

She obeys immediately and completely, which by now is what we expect of her, and she goes to Philistia.

Think about what that costs a woman of standing in Shunem. The Philistines are the old enemy; Israelites went to them for iron and not much else. She takes her household out of the land God gave her family and lives seven years among people her nation had fought for three centuries, because a prophet told her to.

'And at the end of the seven years, when the woman returned from the land of the Philistines, she went to appeal to the king for her house and her land.'

Seven years is a long absence. The house has been occupied or the land taken over or the crown has absorbed it, and she has to go to court to get it back — a widow, apparently, since her elderly husband is not mentioned again, with no one to represent her.

'Now the king was talking with Gehazi the servant of the man of God, saying, "Tell me all the great things that Elisha has done."'

Here is a difficulty, and it should be stated rather than slid past. Gehazi was struck with leprosy in chapter 5 and went out from Elisha's presence white as snow, and a leper does not sit making conversation with the king of Israel.

The first verse of this chapter has already told us we are looking backwards, so the episode may belong to an earlier period; or the exclusion may not have been enforced in the northern court, which kept golden calves and a Baal temple and was not scrupulous about the law of Moses. The text does not say. It is better to leave it open than to manufacture an answer.

What is clear is the king's subject. He wants the Elisha stories, all of them, and he has sent for the man who was there.

'And while he was telling the king how Elisha had restored the dead to life, behold, the woman whose son he had restored to life appealed to the king for her house and her land. And Gehazi said, "My lord, O king, here is the woman, and here is her son whom Elisha restored to life."'

Read the timing of that again.

Not on the same day. Not during the same conversation. While he was telling the king how Elisha had restored the dead to life — in the middle of that sentence, in that minute, the woman whose son it was walks into the room with the boy beside her.

She has come about a property claim. She has no idea what is being discussed inside, or that the king is in a mood to hear about Elisha at all, or that the one man in the kingdom who can corroborate her story is standing at the king's elbow. She has walked up the steps of a palace to ask a favour of a man who is not known for granting them, and the door opens on the one moment in seven years when her case has already been made for her.

Now put that beside what she said in chapter 4. Elisha had offered her exactly this: would you have a word spoken on your behalf to the king or to the commander of the army? And she said no. I dwell among my own people — I have family here, I am not a petitioner, I want nothing (4:13).

Years later she is a petitioner, and she needs the introduction she turned down.

What she gets is better than what she refused. She does not have to produce a letter or invoke a name or explain who she is. Somebody is already telling the king her story, with enthusiasm, as the best thing he knows — and she and the living evidence walk in on the sentence.

She had declined a patron. God had one in the room.

'And when the king asked the woman, she told him. So the king appointed an official for her, saying, "Restore all that was hers, together with all the produce of the fields from the day that she left the land until now."'

She gets it all back, and then something nobody asked for: seven years of harvests, calculated from the day she left.

The king assigns an officer to see it done, which means somebody with authority walks back to Shunem with her and puts her in possession. It is a thorough, administrative, entirely un-miraculous piece of justice, and it is the ending of a story that began with a prophet telling a woman to leave her home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — The Man of God Wept
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elisha turns up in Damascus, and the king of Syria sends forty camel-loads of presents to ask through him whether he will recover (vv. 7-9). The answer has two halves: go, say to him, 'You shall certainly recover,' but the LORD has shown me that he shall certainly die (v. 10). Then a long stare, until Hazael is squirming, and the man of God wept (v. 11) — because he has been shown what this man will do: fortresses burned, young men killed, little ones dashed in pieces, pregnant women ripped open (v. 12). What is your servant, who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing? (v. 13). And the next day he holds a wet cloth over his master's face until he is dead (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The two halves of verse 10 are both true and neither is a lie. The illness is not going to kill Ben-hadad — he would certainly recover from it. Something else is going to kill him, and it is standing in the room holding the message. Elisha hands a man a sentence and watches what he does with it, and what Hazael does is deliver the first half and act on the second.
verseByVerse.examples: And Elisha weeps. That is the answer to a question people put about God's foreknowledge — whether knowing what is coming makes him cold about it. His prophet is shown the atrocities of the next thirty years in advance and stands in a room in Damascus crying about children who have not been born yet.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Elisha came to Damascus. Ben-hadad the king of Syria was sick. And when it was told him, "The man of God has come here," the king said to Hazael, "Take a present with you and go to meet the man of God, and inquire of the LORD through him, saying, 'Shall I recover from this sickness?'" So Hazael went to meet him, and took a present with him, all kinds of goods of Damascus, forty camels' loads. When he came and stood before him, he said, "Your son Ben-hadad king of Syria has sent me to you, saying, 'Shall I recover from this sickness?'" And Elisha said to him, "Go, say to him, 'You shall certainly recover,' but the LORD has shown me that he shall certainly die." And he fixed his gaze and stared at him, until he was embarrassed. And the man of God wept. And Hazael said, "Why does my lord weep?" He answered, "Because I know the evil that you will do to the people of Israel. You will set on fire their fortresses, and you will kill their young men with the sword and dash in pieces their little ones and rip open their pregnant women." And Hazael said, "What is your servant, who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing?" Elisha answered, "The LORD has shown me that you are to be king over Syria." Then he departed from Elisha and came to his master, who said to him, "What did Elisha say to you?" And he answered, "He told me that you would certainly recover." But the next day he took the bed cloth and dipped it in water and spread it over his face, till he died. And Hazael became king in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Elisha came to Damascus. Ben-hadad the king of Syria was sick. And when it was told him, "The man of God has come here,"'

The prophet of Israel walks into the capital of the country that has been besieging Samaria, and the first thing that happens is that the king asks to consult him.

That is Naaman's doing, at one remove. The commander of that army went home clean and told everybody, and years later the throne of Syria takes it for granted that the God of Israel answers through this man.

'the king said to Hazael, "Take a present with you and go to meet the man of God, and inquire of the LORD through him, saying, 'Shall I recover from this sickness?'"'

The question is Ahaziah's question, word for word in substance, from the first chapter of this book: shall I recover from this sickness? The king of Israel sent to a Philistine shrine and was told he would die. The king of Syria sends to the prophet of Israel.

'So Hazael went to meet him, and took a present with him, all kinds of goods of Damascus, forty camels' loads. When he came and stood before him, he said, "Your son Ben-hadad king of Syria has sent me to you, saying, 'Shall I recover from this sickness?'"'

Forty camel-loads, and the king of Syria calling himself your son in a message to an Israelite prophet.

'And Elisha said to him, "Go, say to him, 'You shall certainly recover,' but the LORD has shown me that he shall certainly die."'

This verse looks at first like an instruction to lie, and it is not.

Two things are being said, and both are true. The sickness is not fatal — Ben-hadad would certainly get over it. And Ben-hadad is certainly going to die, because the man standing in front of Elisha holding the enquiry is going to kill him tomorrow.

Elisha is not composing a deception. He is handing a message to a man and watching what he does with it, and the reader is being told in advance what he will do: he will deliver the first half and act on the second.

(An honest note for anyone comparing translations: the Hebrew here carries a variant, and the traditional reading of the written text is say to him, you shall not recover, while the reading the scribes marked for pronunciation gives what the ESV prints. The sense of the verse as a whole is unaffected — either way the sickness is not what kills him.)

'And he fixed his gaze and stared at him, until he was embarrassed. And the man of God wept.'

Nothing happens in this verse except a look, and it is one of the most uncomfortable moments in Scripture.

The prophet sets his face and stares at Hazael, and holds it, and goes on holding it past the point where either man could pretend it was accidental, until the Syrian officer cannot stand it any longer. And then he starts to cry.

Hazael has come with a routine diplomatic errand and forty camels, and he is standing in front of a foreign holy man who will not stop looking at him and has begun to weep.

'And Hazael said, "Why does my lord weep?" He answered, "Because I know the evil that you will do to the people of Israel. You will set on fire their fortresses, and you will kill their young men with the sword and dash in pieces their little ones and rip open their pregnant women."'

He has been shown it, and he names it in four clauses, and there is nothing softened in any of them.

These are not rhetorical horrors. Amos will indict Damascus by name for precisely this kind of campaign a century later (Amos 1:3-5), and this book will record the results twice over — Hazael cutting Israel down until Jehoahaz had fifty horsemen left (10:32-33; 13:7).

Now take what the verse says about God, because it answers something people genuinely worry about. If God knows the future, does he not therefore watch it coldly, the way a man watches a play he has already seen? Here is a man who has been let in on it, and the effect of foreknowledge on him is tears. He is standing in a room in Damascus weeping over children who have not been conceived yet. Knowing in advance did not make it smaller.

'And Hazael said, "What is your servant, who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing?" Elisha answered, "The LORD has shown me that you are to be king over Syria."'

His answer has been read two ways, as false modesty and as genuine revulsion, and the second is more likely and more frightening.

He calls himself a dog — a nobody, a servant, a man without the standing to do anything on that scale. And he means it. On the day he heard the list he could not imagine himself doing any of it, and the idea that he might was so far outside his own picture of himself that the only sense he could make of the prophecy was that it must be about something else.

He murders his master the following morning.

That is the thing to carry out of this chapter, and it applies to everybody who has ever said the words I could never. Almost nobody who does a terrible thing was, the week before, a person who thought he might. Between what is your servant, who is but a dog and a wet cloth held over a sick man's face there is one night, one opportunity, and one piece of information he did not have before — that the throne was going to be his.

Elisha's reply supplies exactly that piece of information, and God says it anyway. Hazael was not made a murderer by being told. He was shown what he was, and what he did with it, he chose.

'Then he departed from Elisha and came to his master, who said to him, "What did Elisha say to you?" And he answered, "He told me that you would certainly recover."'

He reports half a sentence, accurately, and the half he leaves out is the half about dying.

It is the most effective kind of lie, because every word of it is true.

'But the next day he took the bed cloth and dipped it in water and spread it over his face, till he died. And Hazael became king in his place.'

The bed cloth. A blanket, dipped in water so that it clings, laid over the face of a sick man who cannot get up.

The writer gives it one flat sentence with no adjectives, which is far worse than any amount of horror would have been.

With that, an instruction given on Mount Horeb is finally carried out. God told Elijah, in the whisper after the wind and the earthquake and the fire, go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus. And when you arrive, you shall anoint Hazael to be king over Syria (1 Kgs. 19:15). Elijah never went. He called Elisha instead and left the rest of the list to him, and here, a generation later, the successor walks into Damascus and the thing is done — not by anointing, simply by telling a man the truth about himself.

The commission outlived the man who received it. Every item on that list is being worked through, and Jehu is still to come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–29 — For the Daughter of Ahab Was His Wife
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The account crosses to Judah, and the writer supplies the cause in the same breath as the verdict: Jehoram walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife (v. 18). Then the sentence that keeps Judah standing: yet the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever (v. 19). Edom revolts and is not recovered; Libnah goes too (vv. 20-22). His son Ahaziah reigns one year, for he was son-in-law to the house of Ahab (v. 27), and goes north to fight at Ramoth-gilead — and then down to Jezreel to visit his wounded cousin (vv. 28-29).
verseByVerse.theology: That marriage was made in one neutral sentence at the opening of 1 Kings 22, when a good king went north on a friendly visit. Here is the invoice, written by the historian as a causal clause: the reason the house of David began behaving like the house of Ahab is that a daughter of Ahab was in it.
verseByVerse.examples: And the lamp is the only reason there is still a Judah to ruin. It was promised at the tearing of the kingdom — that David my servant may always have a lamp before me (1 Kgs. 11:36) — and kept for Abijam who did not deserve it (15:4), and it is kept here for a man who married Ahab's daughter. Judah survives on a promise made to a dead man about a descendant not yet born.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab, king of Israel, when Jehoshaphat was king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, began to reign. He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever. In his days Edom revolted from the rule of Judah and set up a king of their own. Then Joram passed over to Zair with all his chariots and rose by night, and he and his chariot commanders struck the Edomites who had surrounded him, but his army fled home. So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time. Now the rest of the acts of Joram, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? So Joram slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place. In the twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab, king of Israel, Ahaziah the son of Jehoram, king of Judah, began to reign. Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah; she was a granddaughter of Omri king of Israel. He also walked in the way of the house of Ahab and did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done, for he was son-in-law to the house of Ahab. He went with Joram the son of Ahab to make war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead, and the Syrians wounded Joram. And King Joram returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that the Syrians had given him at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab, king of Israel, when Jehoshaphat was king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, began to reign.'

'He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.'

The account crosses the border to Judah, and the reader should brace, because this is the reign where the infection reaches the house of David.

'And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.'

There is the causal clause, written by the historian himself, and it is the invoice for a decision made two books' worth of pages ago.

In the opening verse of 1 Kings 22, a good king of Judah went north on a friendly visit to Ahab, and the writer recorded it as a piece of diplomatic news. Chronicles supplies the detail: he made a marriage alliance with Ahab (2 Chron. 18:1). Jehoshaphat's son married Ahab's daughter, and everybody at the time would have called it statesmanship — the end of two generations of hostility between brothers.

Here is the consequence, stated as a reason: the king of Judah behaved like the kings of Israel for the daughter of Ahab was his wife.

Chronicles adds what Kings leaves out about this man: he murdered all six of his brothers when he came to the throne (2 Chron. 21:4). That is the house of Ahab's method arriving in Jerusalem inside one generation.

'Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.'

The lamp.

The reader of these two books has met it twice before and should stop here. When the kingdom was torn away from Solomon, God kept one tribe for his son that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem (1 Kgs. 11:36). When Abijam reigned and his heart was not whole, the lamp was the reason he survived — for David's sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem (1 Kgs. 15:4). And here it is again, in the reign of a man who married Ahab's daughter and killed his own brothers.

Take the picture seriously, because it is a small one and deliberately so. Not a fire, not a beacon — a lamp, the clay dish with a wick in it that a household kept burning through the night so that the house was never wholly dark. It does not illuminate much. It only refuses to go out.

Notice on what ground it is kept burning. Not for Jehoram's sake, obviously. Not because Judah is better than Israel; the writer has just said Judah is behaving exactly like Israel. For the sake of David his servant, since he promised.

The nation is being carried by an oath sworn to a man who has been dead for a century and a half, about descendants who had not been born when it was sworn. That is the only reason there is still a Judah at all, and the comfort in it should be put plainly: the promises God makes are not maintained by the quality of the people who inherit them.

The lamp does not go out. It will gutter through Athaliah, who is about to try to extinguish the whole line, and be down to one baby hidden in a bedroom in the temple. It goes into exile and comes back. And at the end of the Bible the one who was promised says of himself, I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star (Rev. 22:16).

'In his days Edom revolted from the rule of Judah and set up a king of their own.'

'Then Joram passed over to Zair with all his chariots and rose by night, and he and his chariot commanders struck the Edomites who had surrounded him, but his army fled home.'

'So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time.'

A night attack by the king and his chariot officers, and the infantry runs. He breaks out of an encirclement and loses the war, and the writer records the outcome twice: Edom is gone, and gone permanently.

Libnah goes at the same time, and Libnah is not a foreign vassal — it is a town in Judah's own territory. The kingdom is coming apart at the edges and in the middle at once.

'Now the rest of the acts of Joram, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?'

'So Joram slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.'

'In the twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab, king of Israel, Ahaziah the son of Jehoram, king of Judah, began to reign.'

'Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah; she was a granddaughter of Omri king of Israel.'

The formula in Judah always names the mother, and this time the name matters more than any other in the book.

Athaliah. Ahab's daughter, Jezebel's daughter, Omri's granddaughter, and the queen mother of Judah. She has been in Jerusalem for twenty years. Her husband is dead and her son is twenty-two and on the throne and will reign for one year.

Keep her in view. When that year is over she will do the thing nobody in Israel or Judah had ever attempted, and the lamp of verse 19 will come down to a single infant.

'He also walked in the way of the house of Ahab and did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done, for he was son-in-law to the house of Ahab.'

The same explanation twice in one chapter, for father and son. The historian is not interested in subtlety here. He states the cause both times, in the same words, in case anyone thought the first was incidental.

'He went with Joram the son of Ahab to make war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead, and the Syrians wounded Joram.'

Ramoth-gilead. The reader has been here before.

It is the town Ahab went to war for on the strength of four hundred prophets and a lying spirit, and where an arrow shot by a man aiming at nobody found the join in his armour. Now his son is fighting at the same place, against the man Elisha wept over, with a king of Judah beside him — exactly as Ahab had a king of Judah beside him.

The families are repeating themselves at the same address.

'And King Joram returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that the Syrians had given him at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was sick.'

Look where everyone has ended up, and notice that the writer has done it deliberately.

The king of Israel is lying wounded in Jezreel. The king of Judah, his nephew, has come down to visit him and is in the same house. The queen mother of the north, Jezebel, is in that town. And Jezebel's daughter is sitting in Jerusalem waiting for news.

Jezreel is where Naboth had a vineyard. It is the ground Elijah stood on to tell Ahab that dogs would lick his blood in the place where they licked Naboth's, and that the dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of that same town (1 Kgs. 21:19, 23). The sentence was deferred, not cancelled — in his son's days I will bring the disaster (21:29).

Every person named in that sentence is now in Jezreel or one day's ride from it, and the last item on the list God gave Elijah at Horeb is an officer in the army at Ramoth-gilead.

8.theology:
The timing (vv. 4-5). Not the same day — the same sentence. She arrives to argue a property claim while a servant is mid-story about the raising of her own son, and never has to make her case. And she is the woman who had refused exactly this introduction when it was offered (4:13). What she declined out of contentment, God supplied out of kindness, better than the version on offer.

An honest difficulty (v. 4). Gehazi is a leper (5:27) and is conversing with the king. Verse 1 has already marked this as a flashback, and Kings does not always run in order; or the northern court may simply not have enforced the law. The text does not say, and saying so is better than manufacturing an answer.

Both halves true (v. 10). The sickness will not kill Ben-hadad; Hazael will. Elisha is not composing a lie but handing a man a message and watching what he does with it — and Hazael delivers the first half and acts on the second.

Foreknowledge and tears (vv. 11-12). The question people actually worry about is whether knowing the future makes God cold about it. His prophet is let in on thirty years of atrocity and stands in a room in Damascus weeping over children not yet conceived. Knowing in advance did not make it smaller.

I could never (v. 13). What is your servant, who is but a dog? is most likely genuine, and that is what makes it frightening. Almost nobody who does a terrible thing was, the week before, a man who thought he might. Between that sentence and the wet cloth there is one night, one opportunity, and one new piece of information. God gave him the information; what he did with it, he chose.

A commission outliving the man (v. 15). On Horeb, Elijah was told to anoint Hazael king over Syria (1 Kgs. 19:15) and never did it. A generation later his successor walks into Damascus and it is done — without an anointing, simply by telling a man the truth about himself.

For the daughter of Ahab was his wife (v. 18). The historian's own causal clause, and the invoice for a friendly state visit recorded neutrally in 1 Kings 22:1. Said twice in one chapter, of father and son, in case anyone thought the first mention was incidental.

The lamp (v. 19). Third appearance: 1 Kings 11:36 at the tearing of the kingdom, 1 Kings 15:4 for a king whose heart was not whole, and here for a man who married Ahab's daughter and murdered his brothers. It is a small picture on purpose — the clay dish a household kept alight all night so the house was never wholly dark. It does not illuminate much; it refuses to go out. And it is kept burning for the sake of a man dead a century and a half, about descendants unborn when the promise was made. God's promises are not maintained by the quality of the people who inherit them.
8.examples:
Then: A woman came home after seven years in enemy country to find strangers on her land, walked up the steps of a palace to beg for it back, and opened the door on the one minute in seven years when the king was being told her own son's story by the one man who could confirm it.

Now: Three things. First, her introduction. She had turned down a word in the king's ear because she wanted nothing and owed nothing, and years later she needed precisely that — and got a better version of it than the one she refused. Contentment that declines a favour is not thereby left unprovided for. Second, Hazael. The sentence to be afraid of in your own mouth is I could never, because the man who said it in this chapter meant it, and did it the following morning. What stood between him and the act was not character but circumstance. Third, the lamp. If you are measuring whether God will keep faith with you by the state of your own obedience this month, notice who the lamp was being kept for in verse 19, and on whose account.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets and said to him, "Tie up your garments, and take this flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead.<sup>2</sup>And when you arrive, look there for Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. And go in and have him rise from among his fellows, and lead him to an inner chamber.<sup>3</sup>Then take the flask of oil and pour it on his head and say, 'Thus says the LORD, I anoint you king over Israel.' Then open the door and flee; do not linger."<sup>4</sup>So the young man, the servant of the prophet, went to Ramoth-gilead.<sup>5</sup>And when he came, behold, the commanders of the army were in council. And he said, "I have a word for you, O commander." And Jehu said, "To which of us all?" And he said, "To you, O commander."<sup>6</sup>So he arose and went into the house. And the young man poured the oil on his head, saying to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, I anoint you king over the people of the LORD, over Israel.<sup>7</sup>And you shall strike down the house of Ahab your master, so that I may avenge on Jezebel the blood of my servants the prophets, and the blood of all the servants of the LORD.<sup>8</sup>For the whole house of Ahab shall perish, and I will cut off from Ahab every male, bond or free, in Israel.<sup>9</sup>And I will make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah.<sup>10</sup>And the dogs shall eat Jezebel in the territory of Jezreel, and none shall bury her." Then he opened the door and fled.<sup>11</sup>When Jehu came out to the servants of his master, they said to him, "Is all well? Why did this mad fellow come to you?" And he said to them, "You know the fellow and his talk."<sup>12</sup>And they said, "That is not true; tell us now." And he said, "Thus and so he spoke to me, saying, 'Thus says the LORD, I anoint you king over Israel.'"<sup>13</sup>Then in haste every man of them took his garment and put it under him on the bare steps, and they blew the trumpet and proclaimed, "Jehu is king."<sup>14</sup>Thus Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi conspired against Joram. (Now Joram with all Israel had been on guard at Ramoth-gilead against Hazael king of Syria,<sup>15</sup>but King Joram had returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that the Syrians had given him, when he fought with Hazael king of Syria.) So Jehu said, "If this is your decision, then let no one slip out of the city to go and tell the news in Jezreel."<sup>16</sup>Then Jehu mounted his chariot and went to Jezreel, for Joram lay there. And Ahaziah king of Judah had come down to visit Joram.<sup>17</sup>Now the watchman was standing on the tower in Jezreel, and he saw the company of Jehu as he came and said, "I see a company." And Joram said, "Take a horseman and send to meet them, and let him say, 'Is it peace?'"<sup>18</sup>So a man on horseback went to meet him and said, "Thus says the king, 'Is it peace?'" And Jehu said, "What do you have to do with peace? Turn around and ride behind me." And the watchman reported, saying, "The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back."<sup>19</sup>Then he sent out a second horseman, who came to them and said, "Thus the king has said, 'Is it peace?'" And Jehu answered, "What do you have to do with peace? Turn around and ride behind me."<sup>20</sup>Again the watchman reported, "He reached them, but he is not coming back. And the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi, for he drives furiously."<sup>21</sup>Joram said, "Make ready." And they made ready his chariot. Then Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah set out, each in his chariot, and went to meet Jehu, and met him at the property of Naboth the Jezreelite.<sup>22</sup>And when Joram saw Jehu, he said, "Is it peace, Jehu?" He answered, "What peace can there be, so long as the whorings and the sorceries of your mother Jezebel are so many?"<sup>23</sup>Then Joram reined about and fled, saying to Ahaziah, "Treachery, O Ahaziah!"<sup>24</sup>And Jehu drew his bow with his full strength, and shot Joram between the shoulders, so that the arrow pierced his heart, and he sank in his chariot.<sup>25</sup>Jehu said to Bidkar his aide, "Take him up and throw him on the plot of ground belonging to Naboth the Jezreelite. For remember, when you and I rode side by side behind Ahab his father, how the LORD made this pronouncement against him:<sup>26</sup>'As surely as I saw yesterday the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons—declares the LORD—I will repay you on this plot of ground.' Now therefore take him up and throw him on the plot of ground, in accordance with the word of the LORD."<sup>27</sup>When Ahaziah the king of Judah saw this, he fled in the direction of Beth-haggan. And Jehu pursued him and said, "Shoot him also." And they shot him in the chariot at the ascent of Gur, which is by Ibleam. And he fled to Megiddo and died there.<sup>28</sup>His servants carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem, and buried him in his tomb with his fathers in the city of David.<sup>29</sup>In the eleventh year of Joram the son of Ahab, Ahaziah began to reign over Judah.<sup>30</sup>When Jehu came to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it. And she painted her eyes and adorned her head and looked out of the window.<sup>31</sup>And as Jehu entered the gate, she said, "Is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master?"<sup>32</sup>And he lifted up his face to the window and said, "Who is on my side? Who?" Two or three eunuchs looked out at him.<sup>33</sup>He said, "Throw her down." So they threw her down. And some of her blood spattered on the wall and on the horses, and they trampled on her.<sup>34</sup>Then he went in and ate and drank. And he said, "See now to this cursed woman and bury her, for she is a king's daughter."<sup>35</sup>But when they went to bury her, they found no more of her than the skull and the feet and the palms of her hands.<sup>36</sup>When they came back and told him, he said, "This is the word of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Elijah the Tishbite: 'In the territory of Jezreel the dogs shall eat the flesh of Jezebel,<sup>37</sup>and the corpse of Jezebel shall be as dung on the face of the field in the territory of Jezreel, so that no one can say, This is Jezebel.'"
9.overview:
The last item on the list God gave Elijah at Horeb is carried out by a student whose name we never learn, sent alone into a council of army commanders with a flask of oil and an instruction to run afterwards. Inside a minute the cloaks are on the steps and the trumpet has gone.

What follows is fast, professional and exact. A news blackout; a drive to Jezreel; a watchman on a tower reporting a dust cloud, then a swallowed messenger, then another, and then a style of driving he recognises at a distance. Is it peace? is asked five times in this chapter, and verse 22 answers all of them: there is none to be had while what Jezebel introduced is still running.

The two kings drive out and meet him on the plot of ground Naboth would not sell. An arrow drawn at full strength does what an arrow drawn at random did to Ahab, and Jehu — who was a junior officer in the escort the day Elijah pronounced the sentence — quotes the oracle from memory over the body. Then Jezebel paints her face, calls him Zimri from an upper window, and is thrown down by her own household while he goes in to lunch.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Open the Door and Flee
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elisha does not go himself. He hands a flask of oil to an unnamed student and sends him to Ramoth-gilead with instructions that end then open the door and flee; do not linger (v. 3). The young man walks into a council of army commanders, asks for Jehu, anoints him in an inner room with the full commission — you shall strike down the house of Ahab your master, so that I may avenge on Jezebel the blood of my servants the prophets (v. 7) — and runs. The officers ask why this mad fellow came; Jehu is evasive, then tells them; and inside one verse they have thrown their cloaks on the bare steps, blown the trumpet and proclaimed him king (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The last item on the list God gave Elijah on Horeb — Hazael, Jehu, Elisha (1 Kgs. 19:16) — is carried out by a man whose name we are never told, who was chosen for it, sent on foot into a room full of generals, and told to run for his life afterwards.
verseByVerse.examples: And note what the soldiers call him. Meshugga — this madman. That was the officer class's settled view of prophets, and Hosea records that it was general: the prophet is a fool, the man of the spirit is mad (Hos. 9:7). Jehu agrees with them — you know the fellow and his talk — with the oil still wet in his hair.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets and said to him, "Tie up your garments, and take this flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead. And when you arrive, look there for Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. And go in and have him rise from among his fellows, and lead him to an inner chamber. Then take the flask of oil and pour it on his head and say, 'Thus says the LORD, I anoint you king over Israel.' Then open the door and flee; do not linger." So the young man, the servant of the prophet, went to Ramoth-gilead. And when he came, behold, the commanders of the army were in council. And he said, "I have a word for you, O commander." And Jehu said, "To which of us all?" And he said, "To you, O commander." So he arose and went into the house. And the young man poured the oil on his head, saying to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, I anoint you king over the people of the LORD, over Israel. And you shall strike down the house of Ahab your master, so that I may avenge on Jezebel the blood of my servants the prophets, and the blood of all the servants of the LORD. For the whole house of Ahab shall perish, and I will cut off from Ahab every male, bond or free, in Israel. And I will make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah. And the dogs shall eat Jezebel in the territory of Jezreel, and none shall bury her." Then he opened the door and fled. When Jehu came out to the servants of his master, they said to him, "Is all well? Why did this mad fellow come to you?" And he said to them, "You know the fellow and his talk." And they said, "That is not true; tell us now." And he said, "Thus and so he spoke to me, saying, 'Thus says the LORD, I anoint you king over Israel.'" Then in haste every man of them took his garment and put it under him on the bare steps, and they blew the trumpet and proclaimed, "Jehu is king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets and said to him, "Tie up your garments, and take this flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead.'

Elisha does not go.

The last commission on the list God gave Elijah in the whisper at Horeb — Hazael over Syria, Jehu over Israel, Elisha in your place (1 Kgs. 19:15-16) — is the most dangerous errand in the kingdom, and the prophet hands it to a student and stays home.

Tie up your garments means hitch your robe so you can run. It is the same instruction he gave Gehazi on the road to the Shunammite's house, and it means the same thing here.

'And when you arrive, look there for Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. And go in and have him rise from among his fellows, and lead him to an inner chamber.'

'Then take the flask of oil and pour it on his head and say, 'Thus says the LORD, I anoint you king over Israel.' Then open the door and flee; do not linger."'

Take the shape of that instruction seriously, because it is not a ceremony, it is a raid.

Walk into a building full of the senior officers of an army in the field. Pick one of them out by name in front of the others. Get him alone. Pour oil on his head and tell him he is king — which is treason, and which every man in the next room is close enough to hear about within a minute. Then open the door and run, and do not stop to see what happens.

We are never told this young man's name. He is one of the students from the overcrowded house by the Jordan, and he does it.

'So the young man, the servant of the prophet, went to Ramoth-gilead.'

'And when he came, behold, the commanders of the army were in council. And he said, "I have a word for you, O commander." And Jehu said, "To which of us all?" And he said, "To you, O commander."'

The exchange is beautifully done. He announces himself to a room of ranking officers; Jehu asks which of them he means; and the boy says: you.

'So he arose and went into the house. And the young man poured the oil on his head, saying to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, I anoint you king over the people of the LORD, over Israel.'

'And you shall strike down the house of Ahab your master, so that I may avenge on Jezebel the blood of my servants the prophets, and the blood of all the servants of the LORD.'

The ground of the commission is stated, and it is not politics. It is blood.

The blood of my servants the prophets. The reader was told about that in a parenthesis, long ago and almost in passing: when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the LORD, Obadiah hid a hundred of them in two caves and fed them (1 Kgs. 18:4). The ones he did not reach were killed, and nobody counted them, and nothing in the narrative was done about it for thirty years.

God kept the account. This is what a delayed judgment looks like from the inside: decades in which nothing appears to be happening, and then a young man with a flask of oil.

'For the whole house of Ahab shall perish, and I will cut off from Ahab every male, bond or free, in Israel.'

'And I will make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah.'

'And the dogs shall eat Jezebel in the territory of Jezreel, and none shall bury her." Then he opened the door and fled.'

Every clause of that is quoted from what Elijah said in a vineyard thirteen years before — the house made like Jeroboam's and Baasha's, every male cut off, the dogs eating Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel (1 Kgs. 21:21-24). Nothing has been added and nothing softened. The sentence has simply been waiting.

Then the boy runs, exactly as instructed.

'When Jehu came out to the servants of his master, they said to him, "Is all well? Why did this mad fellow come to you?" And he said to them, "You know the fellow and his talk."'

The word they use is meshugga — a madman, a lunatic. That is what the officers' mess thought of prophets, and it was not an unusual view: Hosea complains that the nation said exactly this — the prophet is a fool, the man of the spirit is mad (Hos. 9:7).

Jehu joins in. You know the fellow and his talk — you know what they are like. He has oil running down his hair from a word of God he has just accepted, and his first public act is to laugh at the messenger with the men who despise him.

Keep that in mind. This man is going to execute the judgment of God with total efficiency and quote the Scriptures accurately while he does it, and the writer has shown us in his second sentence what he is.

'And they said, "That is not true; tell us now." And he said, "Thus and so he spoke to me, saying, 'Thus says the LORD, I anoint you king over Israel.'"'

'Then in haste every man of them took his garment and put it under him on the bare steps, and they blew the trumpet and proclaimed, "Jehu is king."'

The speed is the point. There is no discussion, no delegation sent to sound out the other commanders, no hesitation at all — cloaks come off and go down on the stone steps, a trumpet sounds, and the army has a new king inside a minute.

The house of Ahab has been in power for forty years and it takes one flask of oil and one sentence to end it, because the army had been ready for a long time and nobody had said so out loud.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–29 — At the Property of Naboth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehu seals the town so no word can reach Jezreel, and drives. The watchman reports a company, then a messenger who does not come back, then a second, and then the line that gives him away: the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi, for he drives furiously (v. 20). Two kings ride out to meet him — and met him at the property of Naboth the Jezreelite (v. 21).
