Is it peace, Jehu? — what peace can there be, so long as the whorings and the sorceries of your mother Jezebel are so many? (v. 22). He draws his bow at full strength and shoots Joram through the heart, and has the body thrown onto Naboth's ground, quoting the oracle he heard pronounced in person (vv. 24-26). Ahaziah of Judah is shot too and dies at Megiddo (vv. 27-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Count the question. Is it peace? is asked five times in this chapter (vv. 17, 18, 19, 22, 31), and verse 22 is the answer to all of them. Peace is not the absence of fighting; there is none available while what Jezebel introduced is still running. There is no peace, says my God, for the wicked (Isa. 57:21).
verseByVerse.examples: And set the two arrows side by side. Ahab was killed by a man who drew his bow at random, not aiming at anybody (1 Kgs. 22:34). His son is killed by a man who drew his bow with his full strength and put it between the shoulders. One arrow aimed at nobody and one aimed precisely, and both found the man God had sentenced.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi conspired against Joram. (Now Joram with all Israel had been on guard at Ramoth-gilead against Hazael king of Syria, but King Joram had returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that the Syrians had given him, when he fought with Hazael king of Syria.) So Jehu said, "If this is your decision, then let no one slip out of the city to go and tell the news in Jezreel." Then Jehu mounted his chariot and went to Jezreel, for Joram lay there. And Ahaziah king of Judah had come down to visit Joram. Now the watchman was standing on the tower in Jezreel, and he saw the company of Jehu as he came and said, "I see a company." And Joram said, "Take a horseman and send to meet them, and let him say, 'Is it peace?'" So a man on horseback went to meet him and said, "Thus says the king, 'Is it peace?'" And Jehu said, "What do you have to do with peace? Turn around and ride behind me." And the watchman reported, saying, "The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back." Then he sent out a second horseman, who came to them and said, "Thus the king has said, 'Is it peace?'" And Jehu answered, "What do you have to do with peace? Turn around and ride behind me." Again the watchman reported, "He reached them, but he is not coming back. And the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi, for he drives furiously." Joram said, "Make ready." And they made ready his chariot. Then Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah set out, each in his chariot, and went to meet Jehu, and met him at the property of Naboth the Jezreelite. And when Joram saw Jehu, he said, "Is it peace, Jehu?" He answered, "What peace can there be, so long as the whorings and the sorceries of your mother Jezebel are so many?" Then Joram reined about and fled, saying to Ahaziah, "Treachery, O Ahaziah!" And Jehu drew his bow with his full strength, and shot Joram between the shoulders, so that the arrow pierced his heart, and he sank in his chariot. Jehu said to Bidkar his aide, "Take him up and throw him on the plot of ground belonging to Naboth the Jezreelite. For remember, when you and I rode side by side behind Ahab his father, how the LORD made this pronouncement against him: 'As surely as I saw yesterday the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons—declares the LORD—I will repay you on this plot of ground.' Now therefore take him up and throw him on the plot of ground, in accordance with the word of the LORD." When Ahaziah the king of Judah saw this, he fled in the direction of Beth-haggan. And Jehu pursued him and said, "Shoot him also." And they shot him in the chariot at the ascent of Gur, which is by Ibleam. And he fled to Megiddo and died there. His servants carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem, and buried him in his tomb with his fathers in the city of David. In the eleventh year of Joram the son of Ahab, Ahaziah began to reign over Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Thus Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi conspired against Joram. (Now Joram with all Israel had been on guard at Ramoth-gilead against Hazael king of Syria,'

'but King Joram had returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that the Syrians had given him, when he fought with Hazael king of Syria.) So Jehu said, "If this is your decision, then let no one slip out of the city to go and tell the news in Jezreel."'

The first order of the new reign is a news blackout. Seal the town; nobody rides out.

Jehu is a professional, and everything he does from here is fast, correct and effective. Register that early, because efficiency is going to be the whole of his case.

'Then Jehu mounted his chariot and went to Jezreel, for Joram lay there. And Ahaziah king of Judah had come down to visit Joram.'

Both kings in one town, one of them wounded in bed, the other on a family visit. The writer arranged that at the end of the last chapter and now collects on it.

'Now the watchman was standing on the tower in Jezreel, and he saw the company of Jehu as he came and said, "I see a company." And Joram said, "Take a horseman and send to meet them, and let him say, 'Is it peace?'"'

'So a man on horseback went to meet him and said, "Thus says the king, 'Is it peace?'" And Jehu said, "What do you have to do with peace? Turn around and ride behind me." And the watchman reported, saying, "The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back."'

'Then he sent out a second horseman, who came to them and said, "Thus the king has said, 'Is it peace?'" And Jehu answered, "What do you have to do with peace? Turn around and ride behind me."'

'Again the watchman reported, "He reached them, but he is not coming back. And the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi, for he drives furiously."'

This is one of the best-built passages in the Old Testament, and it works entirely by what a man on a tower can and cannot see.

A dust cloud. A rider goes out and is swallowed. A second rider goes out and is swallowed. And then, as the column gets close enough, the watchman recognises not a face or a standard but a style of driving — and says so.

Jehu drove in a way that could be identified at a distance by a man who had never been near enough to speak to him. Some people are recognisable by the manner of the thing before anybody can make out the substance.

Count the question. Is it peace? — the word is shalom, and it is asked five times in this chapter. Twice by messengers, once in the king's own mouth in three verses' time, and once, at the end, by Jezebel. Everybody in Jezreel wants to know the same thing, and the answer never changes.

'Joram said, "Make ready." And they made ready his chariot. Then Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah set out, each in his chariot, and went to meet Jehu, and met him at the property of Naboth the Jezreelite.'

Stop on the last eight words.

They met him at the property of Naboth the Jezreelite.

Of all the ground outside that town, the two kings drive out and meet the man who has come to kill them on the plot of land a farmer refused to sell, because it was the inheritance of his fathers and not his to give away. Ahab wanted it for a vegetable garden. His wife had the owner and his sons killed by a properly conducted legal procedure with two sworn witnesses. And Elijah met Ahab standing in the rows and said the sentence.

Nobody in either chariot chose that field. The writer simply records where the horses stopped.

'And when Joram saw Jehu, he said, "Is it peace, Jehu?" He answered, "What peace can there be, so long as the whorings and the sorceries of your mother Jezebel are so many?"'

There is the fourth shalom, and here is the answer to all of them.

Joram is asking a diplomatic question — are you loyal, is this a friendly approach. Jehu answers a different and larger one. There is no peace available. Not because of a coup; because of what has been running in this kingdom for forty years and has never been dealt with.

It is exactly what Isaiah says twice over: there is no peace, says my God, for the wicked (Isa. 57:21). Peace is not a mood or a ceasefire. It is being right with God, and where that is missing the quiet is only an interval.

'Then Joram reined about and fled, saying to Ahaziah, "Treachery, O Ahaziah!"'

'And Jehu drew his bow with his full strength, and shot Joram between the shoulders, so that the arrow pierced his heart, and he sank in his chariot.'

Now set this arrow beside the one that killed his father.

At Ramoth-gilead a Syrian soldier drew his bow at random — in his innocence, the Hebrew says, aiming at nobody in particular — and the arrow found the one gap in the armour of the one man in the field who was disguised (1 Kgs. 22:34).

Here a man draws his bow with his full strength, at a named target, at close range, and puts it between the shoulders.

One arrow aimed at nothing and one aimed exactly, and both of them went precisely where God had said. He is not restricted to either method.

'Jehu said to Bidkar his aide, "Take him up and throw him on the plot of ground belonging to Naboth the Jezreelite. For remember, when you and I rode side by side behind Ahab his father, how the LORD made this pronouncement against him:'

Here is the detail that turns this scene from an execution into a memory.

When you and I rode side by side behind Ahab his father.

Jehu was there. He was a junior officer in the escort on the day Ahab drove down to take possession of the vineyard, and he was close enough behind the royal chariot to hear a man in a hair garment step out of the vines and pass sentence on the king. So was Bidkar, who is still riding beside him.

Two young men heard it, and remembered it for years, and one of them is now the instrument of it, and he can still quote it.

'"As surely as I saw yesterday the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons—declares the LORD—I will repay you on this plot of ground." Now therefore take him up and throw him on the plot of ground, in accordance with the word of the LORD."'

Note what his version contains that the account in 1 Kings did not: the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons.

Chapter 21 never mentioned the children. It only made sense that they had died — with an heir alive the land would have reverted to the family and the whole exercise would have been pointless — and here, thirteen years later, in a soldier's recollection of what a prophet said, they are named.

As surely as I saw yesterday. God says it as if it were the previous afternoon.

'When Ahaziah the king of Judah saw this, he fled in the direction of Beth-haggan. And Jehu pursued him and said, "Shoot him also." And they shot him in the chariot at the ascent of Gur, which is by Ibleam. And he fled to Megiddo and died there.'

The king of Judah dies because he was on a family visit.

He had come down to Jezreel to see his cousin, who was his mother's nephew, in the house his grandmother married into. There is nothing in the commission about him; he is collateral in a judgment on somebody else's family. And he is in that chariot because two generations earlier a good king of Judah made a marriage alliance with Ahab and thought it was peace.

'His servants carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem, and buried him in his tomb with his fathers in the city of David.'

He is given a proper burial in the royal tombs, which the kings of Israel in this chapter are not. Chronicles supplies the reason, and it is a striking one: they buried him because they said, He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart (2 Chron. 22:9).

Jehoshaphat's alliance is what put his grandson in that chariot. Jehoshaphat's reputation is what got his body into the family tomb. The man's two legacies met over one corpse.

'In the eleventh year of Joram the son of Ahab, Ahaziah began to reign over Judah.'

A dating note, dropped in at the moment the reign ends. He was twenty-two, and he had one year.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–37 — This Is the Word of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jezebel hears he is coming, paints her eyes, dresses her head and appears at the window (v. 30). Her greeting is a sentence, not a question: is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master? (v. 31). Jehu looks up and asks the room behind her whose side it is on; two or three eunuchs look out; throw her down (vv. 32-33). Then he goes in and has lunch, and afterwards remembers that a king's daughter ought to be buried — and there is nothing left to bury but the skull, the feet and the palms of the hands (vv. 34-35). And Jehu quotes Elijah: so that no one can say, This is Jezebel (vv. 36-37).
verseByVerse.theology: She is not primping. She is a Sidonian king's daughter who has been a queen for forty years, she knows exactly what is coming up the road, and she puts on her face and her headdress to meet it from a window. And she names him accurately: Zimri was the officer who murdered his master and reigned seven days before burning the palace over himself (1 Kgs. 16:9-18). She is not asking how long he will last. She is telling him.
verseByVerse.examples: And her own household throws her out. She had run that palace for four decades, kept eight hundred and fifty prophets at her table and had men killed by letter — and when a stranger in the courtyard called up who is on my side?, the eunuchs in her own room answered by taking hold of her.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jehu came to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it. And she painted her eyes and adorned her head and looked out of the window. And as Jehu entered the gate, she said, "Is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master?" And he lifted up his face to the window and said, "Who is on my side? Who?" Two or three eunuchs looked out at him. He said, "Throw her down." So they threw her down. And some of her blood spattered on the wall and on the horses, and they trampled on her. Then he went in and ate and drank. And he said, "See now to this cursed woman and bury her, for she is a king's daughter." But when they went to bury her, they found no more of her than the skull and the feet and the palms of her hands. When they came back and told him, he said, "This is the word of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Elijah the Tishbite: 'In the territory of Jezreel the dogs shall eat the flesh of Jezebel, and the corpse of Jezebel shall be as dung on the face of the field in the territory of Jezreel, so that no one can say, This is Jezebel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Jehu came to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it. And she painted her eyes and adorned her head and looked out of the window.'

This verse is usually preached as vanity, and it is almost certainly not.

She knows what has happened. Her son is dead on Naboth's field and the man who shot him is driving into the town, and there is no version of the next hour in which she survives it. What she does with the time she has is paint her eyes and dress her head and go to the upper window.

She is a king's daughter of Sidon and she has been queen of this country for forty years, and she is going to meet him as one. It is not seduction; a woman of her age with an army at the gate is not attempting to charm a usurper. It is defiance, and it is the last decision she gets to make.

Say what has to be said about her and say it plainly: she was the most destructive individual in the history of the northern kingdom, she had prophets killed as policy, she had a man and his sons judicially murdered for a field, and she was never once frightened. Courage is not a virtue on its own. It is only ever as good as what it is spent on.

'And as Jehu entered the gate, she said, "Is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master?"'

The fifth shalom, and it is not a question at all.

Zimri is a name every soldier in that courtyard knew. He was the commander of half the chariots who killed his king at dinner, took the throne, and lasted seven days before the army made someone else king and he burned the palace down over his own head (1 Kgs. 16:9-18).

She is not asking whether Jehu comes in peace. She is telling him, in one word, in front of his men, that she has seen this before and that he has a week.

She is the only person in the chapter who is not afraid of him, and she is standing at a window with nothing left.

'And he lifted up his face to the window and said, "Who is on my side? Who?" Two or three eunuchs looked out at him.'

He does not answer her. He looks past her, into the room behind her, and asks the staff.

Two or three faces appear at the window beside hers.

'He said, "Throw her down." So they threw her down. And some of her blood spattered on the wall and on the horses, and they trampled on her.'

Her own household did it.

These are the men who had served her for decades in that palace, who had carried her messages and guarded her door and knew her better than anyone alive. A stranger rode into the courtyard, called up one question, and they took hold of her and put her out of the window.

That is what forty years of rule by fear actually purchases. It buys obedience while there is something to be afraid of, and it buys nothing at all the moment there is something worse in the courtyard. Nobody in that room loved her. They had simply not had a better offer until that morning.

'Then he went in and ate and drank. And he said, "See now to this cursed woman and bury her, for she is a king's daughter."'

He goes in and has a meal.

The queen of Israel is in the street under the horses and Jehu sits down to eat, and it is only afterwards, over the remains of lunch, that it occurs to him that there is a body outside. And notice the reason he gives for burying her. Not decency, and certainly not pity. She is a king's daughter — there is a diplomatic problem with leaving a Sidonian princess in a gateway, and he would rather not have one.

'But when they went to bury her, they found no more of her than the skull and the feet and the palms of her hands.'

'When they came back and told him, he said, "This is the word of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Elijah the Tishbite: 'In the territory of Jezreel the dogs shall eat the flesh of Jezebel,'

'and the corpse of Jezebel shall be as dung on the face of the field in the territory of Jezreel, so that no one can say, This is Jezebel.'"'

The oracle was given in a vineyard by a man in a hair garment who was afterwards taken up in a wind, and it is quoted here by a soldier standing over a skull.

Look at the last clause, because it is the point of the whole horrible scene. So that no one can say, This is Jezebel.

The name had terrified a kingdom for two generations. Kings had been afraid of it, prophets had died because of it, a man had been stoned in his own town on the authority of a letter that carried it. And when they go out to do the one thing that fixes a name to a person — to put a body in a grave with a marker on it — there is not enough left to attach it to.

Then the honest turn, because the reader deserves it and it cuts the other way.

The name did survive. It survived so completely that eight centuries later the risen Christ, writing to a church at Thyatira, could reach for it as the one word that would tell them exactly what was wrong: you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants (Rev. 2:20). He did not have to explain it. They knew.

The woman was erased from the face of a field so thoroughly that nobody could say this is Jezebel. The name outlived her by eight hundred years, as a warning. Both of those are what happened to her, and neither is what she was building.

9.theology:
A delayed judgment, seen from inside (v. 7). The stated ground is the blood of my servants the prophets — killed by Jezebel decades earlier, in a parenthesis the reader was given almost in passing (1 Kgs. 18:4), uncounted and unavenged for thirty years. That is what waiting for God's judgment looks like from the ground: a very long time in which nothing whatever appears to happen, and then a young man with a flask of oil.

This mad fellow (v. 11). Meshugga was the officer class's settled opinion of prophets, and it was general (Hos. 9:7). Jehu agrees with them, with the oil still wet in his hair — which is the writer telling us in his second sentence what this man is, before showing us thirty verses of him executing the word of God with complete accuracy.

Is it peace? (vv. 17, 18, 19, 22, 31). Five times, and the answer is always the same. Joram means are you loyal; Jehu answers the larger question. There is no peace available while that is running — not a mood, not a ceasefire, but being right with God, and where that is missing the quiet is an interval. There is no peace, says my God, for the wicked (Isa. 57:21).

The two arrows. Ahab's killer drew his bow at random, aiming at nobody, and found the one seam in the armour of the one disguised man in the field (1 Kgs. 22:34). His son is killed by a man who drew his bow with his full strength at a named target between the shoulders. God is not restricted to either method.

Jehu was there (vv. 25-26). When you and I rode side by side behind Ahab his father — he was in the escort the day Elijah stepped out of the vines, and he has the oracle word for word thirteen years later. His version even supplies what 1 Kings 21 left out: the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons. And God's own phrase is as surely as I saw yesterday.

Collateral (vv. 27-28). The king of Judah dies on a family visit, inside a judgment on somebody else's house, because two generations earlier a good king made a marriage alliance and called it peace. And he is buried in the royal tombs because he is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart (2 Chron. 22:9). The same man's two legacies met over one body.

What fear buys (vv. 32-33). Her own eunuchs threw her out of the window when a stranger in the courtyard asked one question. Forty years of rule by fear purchases obedience while there is something to be afraid of and nothing at all the moment something worse rides into the yard.

So that no one can say, This is Jezebel (v. 37). When they went to fix her name to a grave there was not enough left to fix it to. And yet the name survived so completely that the risen Christ could use it to a church at Thyatira without explaining it (Rev. 2:20). She was erased from a field and remembered for eight centuries as a warning, and neither of those was what she was building.
9.examples:
Then: A watchman on a tower saw a dust cloud, then a rider go out and not come back, then a second rider go out and not come back — and then recognised the man at the head of the column, before he could make out a face or a standard, purely by the way he drove.

Now: Three things. First, the thirty years. The blood this judgment avenges was shed before most of the people in the chapter were born, and for three decades nothing whatever appeared to be happening about it. If you are waiting on God over something genuinely wicked that nobody has answered for, this chapter is about the shape of that wait, not about its absence. Second, Jehu in verse 11, laughing at the messenger with the men who despise him while the oil is still in his hair. It is entirely possible to accept a commission from God, carry it out accurately, quote the Scriptures correctly throughout, and hold the whole thing in contempt. Third, what Jezebel's household did. She had four decades of absolute obedience from those men and not one of them was hers; the morning something more frightening arrived in the courtyard, they were at the window before he had finished asking.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. So Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria, to the rulers of the city, to the elders, and to the guardians of the sons of Ahab, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Now then, as soon as this letter comes to you, seeing your master's sons are with you, and there are with you chariots and horses, fortified cities also, and weapons,<sup>3</sup>select the best and fittest of your master's sons and set him on his father's throne and fight for your master's house."<sup>4</sup>But they were exceedingly afraid and said, "Behold, the two kings could not stand before him. How then can we stand?"<sup>5</sup>So he who was over the palace, and he who was over the city, together with the elders and the guardians, sent to Jehu, saying, "We are your servants, and we will do all that you tell us. We will not make anyone king. Do whatever is good in your eyes."<sup>6</sup>Then he wrote to them a second letter, saying, "If you are on my side, and if you are ready to obey me, take the heads of your master's sons and come to me at Jezreel tomorrow at this time." Now the king's sons, seventy persons, were with the great men of the city, who were bringing them up.<sup>7</sup>And as soon as the letter came to them, they took the king's sons and slaughtered them, seventy persons, and put their heads in baskets and sent them to him at Jezreel.<sup>8</sup>When the messenger came and told him, "They have brought the heads of the king's sons," he said, "Lay them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until the morning."<sup>9</sup>Then in the morning, when he went out, he stood and said to all the people, "You are innocent. It was I who conspired against my master and killed him, but who struck down all these?<sup>10</sup>Know then that there shall fall to the earth nothing of the word of the LORD, which the LORD spoke concerning the house of Ahab, for the LORD has done what he said by his servant Elijah."<sup>11</sup>So Jehu struck down all who remained of the house of Ahab in Jezreel, all his great men and his close friends and his priests, until he left him none remaining.<sup>12</sup>Then he set out and went to Samaria. On the way, when he was at Beth-eked of the Shepherds,<sup>13</sup>Jehu met the relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah, and he said, "Who are you?" And they answered, "We are the relatives of Ahaziah, and we came down to visit the royal princes and the sons of the queen mother."<sup>14</sup>He said, "Take them alive." And they took them alive and slaughtered them at the pit of Beth-eked, forty-two persons, and he spared none of them.<sup>15</sup>And when he departed from there, he met Jehonadab the son of Rechab coming to meet him. And he greeted him and said to him, "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" And Jehonadab answered, "It is." Jehu said, "If it is, give me your hand." So he gave him his hand. And Jehu took him up with him into the chariot.<sup>16</sup>And he said, "Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD." So he had him ride in his chariot.<sup>17</sup>And when he came to Samaria, he struck down all who remained to Ahab in Samaria, till he had wiped them out, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke to Elijah.<sup>18</sup>Then Jehu assembled all the people and said to them, "Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him much.<sup>19</sup>Now therefore call to me all the prophets of Baal, all his worshipers and all his priests. Let none be missing, for I have a great sacrifice to offer to Baal. Whoever is missing shall not live." But Jehu did it with cunning in order to destroy the worshipers of Baal.<sup>20</sup>And Jehu ordered, "Sanctify a solemn assembly for Baal." So they proclaimed it.<sup>21</sup>And Jehu sent throughout all Israel, and all the worshipers of Baal came, so that there was not a man left who did not come. And they entered the house of Baal, and the house of Baal was filled from one end to the other.<sup>22</sup>He said to him who was in charge of the wardrobe, "Bring out the vestments for all the worshipers of Baal." So he brought out the vestments for them.<sup>23</sup>Then Jehu went into the house of Baal with Jehonadab the son of Rechab, and he said to the worshipers of Baal, "Search, and see that there is no servant of the LORD here among you, but only the worshipers of Baal."<sup>24</sup>Then they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Now Jehu had stationed eighty men outside and said, "The man who allows any of those whom I give into your hands to escape shall forfeit his life."<sup>25</sup>So as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, Jehu said to the guard and to the officers, "Go in and strike them down; let not a man escape." So when they put them to the sword, the guard and the officers cast them out and went into the inner room of the house of Baal,<sup>26</sup>and they brought out the pillar that was in the house of Baal and burned it.<sup>27</sup>And they demolished the pillar of Baal, and demolished the house of Baal, and made it a latrine to this day.<sup>28</sup>Thus Jehu wiped out Baal from Israel.<sup>29</sup>But Jehu did not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin—that is, the golden calves that were in Bethel and in Dan.<sup>30</sup>And the LORD said to Jehu, "Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in my eyes, and have done to the house of Ahab according to all that was in my heart, your sons of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel."<sup>31</sup>But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin.<sup>32</sup>In those days the LORD began to cut off parts of Israel. Hazael defeated them throughout the territory of Israel:<sup>33</sup>from the Jordan eastward, all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites, from Aroer, which is by the Valley of the Arnon, that is, Gilead and Bashan.<sup>34</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jehu and all that he did, and all his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>35</sup>So Jehu slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria. And Jehoahaz his son reigned in his place.<sup>36</sup>The time that Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years.
10.overview:
Jehu writes to the guardians of Ahab's seventy sons daring them to crown a candidate and fight, and they surrender by return of post with a blank cheque — do whatever is good in your eyes. The second letter asks for the heads, and the great families of Samaria, who had been raising those children in their own houses, deliver them in baskets the same day. He never touches one of them: he implicates the entire aristocracy, destroys them as a rival power base, and keeps his hands clean enough to stand at the gate the next morning in front of two heaps of heads and ask the crowd who could have done such a thing.

The theology in his speech is perfectly sound. God had said the house of Ahab would be cut off. God had not said anything about baskets, or staging, or forty-two Judean relatives killed at a cistern on a road because they happened to be travelling.

Then the trap at the temple: a proclaimed festival, compulsory attendance, vestments for everyone, a careful search to be sure no servant of the LORD is inside, eighty men on the door — and the state cult of Baal ends in one morning, with the building turned into the public latrine. Thus Jehu wiped out Baal from Israel. And then the next verse: but Jehu did not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Who Struck Down All These?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehu writes to the guardians of Ahab's seventy sons daring them to pick a candidate and fight — you have chariots and horses, fortified cities also, and weapons (v. 2) — and they capitulate instantly: do whatever is good in your eyes (v. 5). The second letter asks for the heads, and Samaria's own nobility delivers seventy of them in baskets (vv. 6-7). He stacks them in two heaps at the gate overnight, and in the morning tells the town you are innocent... but who struck down all these? and attributes the whole thing to the word of the LORD... by his servant Elijah (vv. 8-10). Then he kills everyone else connected to the house, forty-two Judean relatives on a family visit, and takes Jehonadab the Rechabite into his chariot to see my zeal for the LORD (vv. 11-17).
verseByVerse.theology: He never touches the seventy. He makes the great men of Samaria do it, which implicates the entire aristocracy in the killing and removes them as a rival power base in the same stroke — and then stands at the gate the next morning and asks the crowd who could possibly have done such a thing.
verseByVerse.examples: And the theology he quotes is perfectly sound. God had said the house of Ahab would be cut off and it is being cut off. What God had not said was anything about baskets, or two heaps at a gate, or a speech. The deed was commanded. The manner was his own, and Hosea will call it what it was: I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel (Hos. 1:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. So Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria, to the rulers of the city, to the elders, and to the guardians of the sons of Ahab, saying, "Now then, as soon as this letter comes to you, seeing your master's sons are with you, and there are with you chariots and horses, fortified cities also, and weapons, select the best and fittest of your master's sons and set him on his father's throne and fight for your master's house." But they were exceedingly afraid and said, "Behold, the two kings could not stand before him. How then can we stand?" So he who was over the palace, and he who was over the city, together with the elders and the guardians, sent to Jehu, saying, "We are your servants, and we will do all that you tell us. We will not make anyone king. Do whatever is good in your eyes." Then he wrote to them a second letter, saying, "If you are on my side, and if you are ready to obey me, take the heads of your master's sons and come to me at Jezreel tomorrow at this time." Now the king's sons, seventy persons, were with the great men of the city, who were bringing them up. And as soon as the letter came to them, they took the king's sons and slaughtered them, seventy persons, and put their heads in baskets and sent them to him at Jezreel. When the messenger came and told him, "They have brought the heads of the king's sons," he said, "Lay them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until the morning." Then in the morning, when he went out, he stood and said to all the people, "You are innocent. It was I who conspired against my master and killed him, but who struck down all these? Know then that there shall fall to the earth nothing of the word of the LORD, which the LORD spoke concerning the house of Ahab, for the LORD has done what he said by his servant Elijah." So Jehu struck down all who remained of the house of Ahab in Jezreel, all his great men and his close friends and his priests, until he left him none remaining. Then he set out and went to Samaria. On the way, when he was at Beth-eked of the Shepherds, Jehu met the relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah, and he said, "Who are you?" And they answered, "We are the relatives of Ahaziah, and we came down to visit the royal princes and the sons of the queen mother." He said, "Take them alive." And they took them alive and slaughtered them at the pit of Beth-eked, forty-two persons, and he spared none of them. And when he departed from there, he met Jehonadab the son of Rechab coming to meet him. And he greeted him and said to him, "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" And Jehonadab answered, "It is." Jehu said, "If it is, give me your hand." So he gave him his hand. And Jehu took him up with him into the chariot. And he said, "Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD." So he had him ride in his chariot. And when he came to Samaria, he struck down all who remained to Ahab in Samaria, till he had wiped them out, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke to Elijah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. So Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria, to the rulers of the city, to the elders, and to the guardians of the sons of Ahab, saying,'

Seventy sons means the whole royal clan — sons and grandsons together — and they are being raised by the great families of the capital, which was the ordinary arrangement. Fostering princes out to the nobility tied the aristocracy to the dynasty.

It also, as it turns out, put every one of them in somebody else's house on the day the dynasty fell.

'"Now then, as soon as this letter comes to you, seeing your master's sons are with you, and there are with you chariots and horses, fortified cities also, and weapons,'

'select the best and fittest of your master's sons and set him on his father's throne and fight for your master's house."'

Read the first letter as what it is: a dare, written by a man who is certain it will not be taken.

He lists their assets for them — chariots, horses, fortified cities, weapons — as though helpfully reminding them that they are in a strong position. Pick a candidate. Crown him. Come and fight me.

Jezebel called him Zimri and gave him a week. This letter is the answer to that: he intends to find out immediately whether anyone in Samaria has the nerve, and to settle it before it becomes a war.

'But they were exceedingly afraid and said, "Behold, the two kings could not stand before him. How then can we stand?"'

'So he who was over the palace, and he who was over the city, together with the elders and the guardians, sent to Jehu, saying, "We are your servants, and we will do all that you tell us. We will not make anyone king. Do whatever is good in your eyes."'

Total surrender by return of post, and note the sentence they end on: do whatever is good in your eyes.

They have handed him a blank authority in writing. Whatever he asks next, they have already agreed to it, and he has their signatures.

'Then he wrote to them a second letter, saying, "If you are on my side, and if you are ready to obey me, take the heads of your master's sons and come to me at Jezreel tomorrow at this time." Now the king's sons, seventy persons, were with the great men of the city, who were bringing them up.'

Now the trap closes, and it is well made.

He does not send soldiers to Samaria. He does not go himself. He requires the men who have been raising those boys in their own houses to kill them, and to bring the proof to him.

In one letter he does three things. He disposes of the royal line. He makes every leading family in the capital an accomplice, so that not one of them can ever raise a claim against him or a rebellion in the name of the old house. And he keeps his own hands clean enough to make a speech about it in the morning.

'And as soon as the letter came to them, they took the king's sons and slaughtered them, seventy persons, and put their heads in baskets and sent them to him at Jezreel.'

They do it the same day. The men who had been bringing these children up.

'When the messenger came and told him, "They have brought the heads of the king's sons," he said, "Lay them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until the morning."'

Two heaps, at the gate, overnight.

The gate of a town was not a back alley. It was the public square, the place where the elders sat, the courts met and business was done, and everybody entering or leaving passed through it. He has the baskets emptied into two piles there and left until first light, so that the whole population of Jezreel comes out in the morning and walks into it.

That is not an execution. It is staging.

'Then in the morning, when he went out, he stood and said to all the people, "You are innocent. It was I who conspired against my master and killed him, but who struck down all these?"'

This is one of the most cynical speeches in the Bible and it should be read slowly.

He begins by acquitting the crowd, who have not been accused of anything. Then he admits, frankly, the one crime everybody already knows about — yes, I killed the king. And then he asks, standing in front of two piles of heads that arrived on his own written instructions: but who struck down all these?

The question is unanswerable in public and it is meant to be. The men who did it are the aristocracy of Samaria. They cannot come forward, and he knows it, and he has just told an entire town that somebody else did this.

'Know then that there shall fall to the earth nothing of the word of the LORD, which the LORD spoke concerning the house of Ahab, for the LORD has done what he said by his servant Elijah."'

Then he preaches, and every word of it is true.

God did say the house of Ahab would be cut off, and said it through Elijah, in a vineyard, thirteen years before. Nothing of that word has fallen to the ground. Jehu's doctrine is correct and his text is correct and he is quoting a real prophet accurately.

He is also using it to close down the only question anyone in that square might have asked him.

Be exact about the distinction, since the whole chapter turns on it. The deed was commanded. The manner was not. Nothing God said to Elijah or through the young man with the flask of oil involved tricking the guardians of seventy children into doing it, or stacking the evidence at a gate for effect, or making a speech about providence over the top of it in the morning.

God does not let that pass. Roughly a century later, through Hosea, he names this town and this family: yet a little while, and I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel (Hos. 1:4). The same God who commissioned the judgment prosecutes the man who executed it.

'So Jehu struck down all who remained of the house of Ahab in Jezreel, all his great men and his close friends and his priests, until he left him none remaining.'

Read the list. The house of Ahab, yes — and then his great men and his close friends and his priests.

Great men and close friends are not a dynasty. They are a social circle, and killing them is not the execution of a sentence; it is the ordinary business of a new regime removing everyone who might be loyal to the old one. The commission has been finished and the killing has not stopped.

'Then he set out and went to Samaria. On the way, when he was at Beth-eked of the Shepherds,'

'Jehu met the relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah, and he said, "Who are you?" And they answered, "We are the relatives of Ahaziah, and we came down to visit the royal princes and the sons of the queen mother."'

'He said, "Take them alive." And they took them alive and slaughtered them at the pit of Beth-eked, forty-two persons, and he spared none of them.'

Forty-two men of the royal family of Judah, met by accident on a road.

They are not part of the house of Ahab. They are not in rebellion. They do not even know what has happened — they are on their way north on a courtesy visit to relatives who have been dead for days, and they answer his question openly because they have no reason not to.

He has them taken alive and killed at a cistern.

There is no word from God anywhere in the record that covers this. It is outside the commission by any reading, and the writer records it without comment, in the same flat voice he uses for everything Jehu does, and lets it accumulate.

'And when he departed from there, he met Jehonadab the son of Rechab coming to meet him. And he greeted him and said to him, "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" And Jehonadab answered, "It is." Jehu said, "If it is, give me your hand." So he gave him his hand. And Jehu took him up with him into the chariot.'

Jehonadab repays an introduction. He is the ancestor of the Rechabites, and two and a half centuries later Jeremiah will set jars of wine in front of his descendants in the temple and invite them to drink, and they will refuse, because Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us — and God will hold up their obedience to a dead ancestor as a rebuke to a nation that would not obey a living God (Jer. 35:6-16).

He is a serious man, and Jehu wants him in the chariot.

'And he said, "Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD." So he had him ride in his chariot.'

There is the sentence that gives the whole man away.

Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD.

Zeal that requires a passenger is not zeal. It is performance with a witness in the seat, and Jehu has gone out of his way to collect the most respected religious figure in the district before doing the next thing, so that there will be somebody creditable to say afterwards what he saw.

Nobody who is genuinely burning for the honour of God arranges for an audience first.

'And when he came to Samaria, he struck down all who remained to Ahab in Samaria, till he had wiped them out, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke to Elijah.'

The writer records the fulfilment plainly, as he always does. The word spoken to Elijah has been carried out.

Both things are true at once, and the chapter will not let go of either.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–28 — A Great Sacrifice to Baal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him much (v. 18) — and the writer tells us at once what that is: Jehu did it with cunning in order to destroy the worshipers of Baal (v. 19). A national assembly is proclaimed, the temple fills from one end to the other, vestments are issued to everyone present, and a careful search is made to ensure no servant of the LORD is caught in the building (vv. 20-23). Eighty men wait outside; the burnt offering is completed; and the order is given (vv. 24-25). The pillar is burned, the house pulled down, and the site made a latrine to this day (v. 27). Thus Jehu wiped out Baal from Israel (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The scruple in verse 23 is real and worth noting: he takes trouble to make sure none of the LORD's people are inside when the doors close. He is not indiscriminate. He is, the writer says in plain Hebrew, cunning — and the word is not a compliment.
verseByVerse.examples: And the achievement is real too, which is why the writer states it flatly. The state cult Jezebel imported, with its temple in the capital and its clergy on the palace budget, was ended in a single morning and the building became the public toilet. Nobody else in the history of that kingdom did anything of the kind.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jehu assembled all the people and said to them, "Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him much. Now therefore call to me all the prophets of Baal, all his worshipers and all his priests. Let none be missing, for I have a great sacrifice to offer to Baal. Whoever is missing shall not live." But Jehu did it with cunning in order to destroy the worshipers of Baal. And Jehu ordered, "Sanctify a solemn assembly for Baal." So they proclaimed it. And Jehu sent throughout all Israel, and all the worshipers of Baal came, so that there was not a man left who did not come. And they entered the house of Baal, and the house of Baal was filled from one end to the other. He said to him who was in charge of the wardrobe, "Bring out the vestments for all the worshipers of Baal." So he brought out the vestments for them. Then Jehu went into the house of Baal with Jehonadab the son of Rechab, and he said to the worshipers of Baal, "Search, and see that there is no servant of the LORD here among you, but only the worshipers of Baal." Then they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Now Jehu had stationed eighty men outside and said, "The man who allows any of those whom I give into your hands to escape shall forfeit his life." So as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, Jehu said to the guard and to the officers, "Go in and strike them down; let not a man escape." So when they put them to the sword, the guard and the officers cast them out and went into the inner room of the house of Baal, and they brought out the pillar that was in the house of Baal and burned it. And they demolished the pillar of Baal, and demolished the house of Baal, and made it a latrine to this day. Thus Jehu wiped out Baal from Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Jehu assembled all the people and said to them, "Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him much."'

It is a lie, and the writer does not leave us to work it out.

'Now therefore call to me all the prophets of Baal, all his worshipers and all his priests. Let none be missing, for I have a great sacrifice to offer to Baal. Whoever is missing shall not live." But Jehu did it with cunning in order to destroy the worshipers of Baal.'

The Hebrew word for what he is doing is not neutral. It is the word for craftiness, for taking somebody by the heel, and the writer applies it to him in the middle of the sentence.

One clause guarantees a full house: whoever is missing shall not live. Attendance is compulsory on pain of death, and the whole Baal community of Israel understands that the new king is a more enthusiastic patron than the old one and that absence will be noticed.

'And Jehu ordered, "Sanctify a solemn assembly for Baal." So they proclaimed it.'

'And Jehu sent throughout all Israel, and all the worshipers of Baal came, so that there was not a man left who did not come. And they entered the house of Baal, and the house of Baal was filled from one end to the other.'

Not a man left who did not come. That is the whole point of the operation. The temple Ahab built in Samaria is packed wall to wall with every Baal worshipper in the kingdom, gathered in one building by their own eagerness.

'He said to him who was in charge of the wardrobe, "Bring out the vestments for all the worshipers of Baal." So he brought out the vestments for them.'

Robes issued to everyone attending. It is a generous gesture from a devout new king, and it also means that in an hour's time every man in that building will be identifiable at a glance and nobody will get out by looking like a bystander.

'Then Jehu went into the house of Baal with Jehonadab the son of Rechab, and he said to the worshipers of Baal, "Search, and see that there is no servant of the LORD here among you, but only the worshipers of Baal."'

This scruple is real and should be credited. He takes trouble — public trouble, in front of the congregation — to make certain that no worshipper of the LORD is inside when the doors close.

He is not indiscriminate, and that matters. Whatever else is wrong with this man, he is not simply killing people.

'Then they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Now Jehu had stationed eighty men outside and said, "The man who allows any of those whom I give into your hands to escape shall forfeit his life."'

'So as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, Jehu said to the guard and to the officers, "Go in and strike them down; let not a man escape." So when they put them to the sword, the guard and the officers cast them out and went into the inner room of the house of Baal,'

He waits until the offering is finished.

There is something particularly cold in that detail. He stands through the whole service, in a temple he intends to level, at a sacrifice he has ordered to a god he means to abolish, and gives the signal only when the liturgy is complete.

'and they brought out the pillar that was in the house of Baal and burned it.'

'And they demolished the pillar of Baal, and demolished the house of Baal, and made it a latrine to this day.'

The building Ahab put up in his capital for his wife's god, with its altar and its pillar and its eight hundred and fifty prophets on the palace budget, was pulled down and the site turned into the public lavatory of Samaria, and it was still that when the account was written.

It is a deliberate and permanent insult, of the kind that leaves nothing to be reverent about.

'Thus Jehu wiped out Baal from Israel.'

The writer says it plainly, because it is true and because nobody else ever did it.

Elijah killed four hundred and fifty prophets at the Kishon and the religion carried on with a temple in the capital. Jehoram took down one pillar and kept everything else. Jehu ended the state cult of Baal in the northern kingdom in a single morning, and it did not come back.

That is a real achievement, accomplished by lies, staging and mass killing, and the Bible credits it to him in six words and then spends the next verse telling us what he would not touch.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — But He Did Not Turn Aside
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But Jehu did not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat... that is, the golden calves that were in Bethel and in Dan (v. 29). And God's verdict on him is genuinely double: because you have done well in carrying out what is right in my eyes, and have done to the house of Ahab according to all that was in my heart, your sons of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel (v. 30) — followed immediately by but Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart (v. 31). In his days the losses begin: Hazael takes the whole Transjordan (vv. 32-33). Twenty-eight years, and the longest dynasty the north ever had (vv. 34-36).
verseByVerse.theology: Put verse 28 next to verse 29 and the man is finished in two sentences. He wiped out Baal — the imported god, his predecessor's religion, the thing it cost him nothing to destroy. He kept the golden calves, which were the founding compromise of the northern kingdom and the reason it existed as a separate country. He would be violent about somebody else's sin and would not touch the one holding up his own throne.
verseByVerse.examples: And the reward is real. Four generations on the throne is the longest run in that kingdom's history, given for obedience God calls what is right in my eyes. Hold it beside Hosea's sentence on the same events (Hos. 1:4) and beside Baasha, condemned for being like Jeroboam's house and also because he destroyed it (1 Kgs. 16:7). A man may be the instrument of a judgment, be rewarded for carrying it out, and be answerable for how he did it.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jehu did not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin—that is, the golden calves that were in Bethel and in Dan. And the LORD said to Jehu, "Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in my eyes, and have done to the house of Ahab according to all that was in my heart, your sons of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel." But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin. In those days the LORD began to cut off parts of Israel. Hazael defeated them throughout the territory of Israel: from the Jordan eastward, all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites, from Aroer, which is by the Valley of the Arnon, that is, Gilead and Bashan. Now the rest of the acts of Jehu and all that he did, and all his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? So Jehu slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria. And Jehoahaz his son reigned in his place. The time that Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But Jehu did not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin—that is, the golden calves that were in Bethel and in Dan.'

There it is, and the word the whole chapter has been waiting for is but.

Set the two verses side by side, because together they are the man.

Thus Jehu wiped out Baal from Israel. But Jehu did not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam.

He destroyed the imported god and kept the domestic one. And look at which was which. Baal was Jezebel's religion, his predecessor's project, a Sidonian import that had never been popular outside the court and had been publicly humiliated on Carmel. Tearing it down cost him nothing; it made him the champion of every ordinary Israelite who had resented the Phoenician queen for forty years.

The golden calves at Bethel and Dan were something else. They were installed by the founder of the northern kingdom for the express purpose of stopping Israelites going south to worship in Jerusalem, and they were the reason the north existed as a separate country with its own throne. Touch those, and you are not a reformer; you are a man arguing his own crown out of existence.

So he was ferocious about the sin that belonged to somebody else's regime, and left standing the one that was holding up his.

Nobody should read that as ancient history. The sins we are most willing to be violent about are almost always the ones that cost us nothing to renounce and that our neighbours already dislike. The one to look for is the one that is load-bearing — the arrangement, the income, the reputation, the relationship that would take the roof off if it went.

'And the LORD said to Jehu, "Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in my eyes, and have done to the house of Ahab according to all that was in my heart, your sons of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel."'

God commends him, and the commendation is not faint.

You have done well. What is right in my eyes. According to all that was in my heart. And the reward is the longest dynasty the northern kingdom ever had — Jehu, Jehoahaz, Joash, Jeroboam the second, and Zechariah, four generations on the throne, in a country where a house lasting two reigns was unusual.

Now hold that beside the other thing God says about the same events, and do not let go of either.

A century later Hosea is told to name his first son Jezreel, for in just a little while I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel, and I will put an end to the kingdom of the house of Israel (Hos. 1:4).

The blood of Jezreel. The same town, the same events, the same dynasty — commended here and prosecuted there.

That is not a contradiction, and the reader of these books has met the principle before in as many words. Baasha wiped out the house of Jeroboam, which God had sentenced, and God's charge against him was that he walked in Jeroboam's ways and also because he destroyed it (1 Kgs. 16:7). Being the instrument of a judgment is not the same as being commissioned for every act carried out inside it.

God rewarded what was obedience in what Jehu did. He held him answerable for the letters, the baskets, the two heaps at the gate, the friends and the priests, the forty-two men at the cistern, and the speech.

Anyone who has ever been on the right side of a dispute should sit with that for a while. Being right about the cause does not license the conduct, and God keeps the two accounts separately.

'But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin.'

Not careful, and not with all his heart. He had been meticulous about everything else in this chapter — the timing of the letters, the vestments, the search of the temple, the eighty men on the door. He was capable of great care. He simply did not spend any of it here.

'In those days the LORD began to cut off parts of Israel. Hazael defeated them throughout the territory of Israel:'

'from the Jordan eastward, all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites, from Aroer, which is by the Valley of the Arnon, that is, Gilead and Bashan.'

Elisha stood in a room in Damascus and wept because he had been shown what this man would do, and here it begins.

The whole Transjordan goes: Gilead, Bashan, the territory of Reuben and Gad and half Manasseh, all the way down to the Arnon. It is a third of the kingdom, and it is never recovered.

Notice which country it is. Gilead is where a man came from who walked into Ahab's throne room and said there would be no rain except by his word. Elijah's own hill country is the first part of Israel to be lost.

'Now the rest of the acts of Jehu and all that he did, and all his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?'

'So Jehu slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria. And Jehoahaz his son reigned in his place.'

'The time that Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years.'

Twenty-eight years, a peaceful death, a burial in the capital, and a dynasty that outlasted every other in that kingdom's history.

He got everything he was promised. He was the man who ended Baal in Israel and the man God commended for doing what was right in his eyes, and he was also the man who drove furiously, collected an audience for his zeal, killed forty-two travellers at a cistern, and kept two golden calves standing for twenty-eight years because they were holding up his throne.

The book files both, and does not attempt to make them into one thing.

10.theology:
Verse 28 against verse 29. He destroyed Baal — his predecessor's imported religion, publicly discredited on Carmel, unpopular outside the court, and free to renounce. He kept the golden calves, which were the founding compromise of the northern kingdom and the reason it existed as a separate country with its own throne. He was ferocious about the sin that belonged to somebody else's regime and would not touch the one holding up his own. The sin to look for in yourself is never the one your neighbours already dislike; it is the load-bearing one.

True theology as a laundry (vv. 9-10). You are innocent... but who struck down all these? — asked over heads that arrived on his own written instructions — followed by an accurate quotation of a real prophet. The deed was commanded and the manner was his, and the distinction is the hinge of the chapter.

Commended and prosecuted (v. 30; Hos. 1:4). God says you have done well... according to all that was in my heart and gives him four generations, the longest dynasty the north ever had. A century later he says I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel. Both are about the same events. The principle was stated plainly earlier in these books: Baasha destroyed a house God had sentenced and was charged with walking in Jeroboam's ways and also because he destroyed it (1 Kgs. 16:7). Being the instrument of a judgment is not a commission for every act inside it, and God keeps the two accounts separately.

Come and see my zeal (v. 16). He detours to collect the most respected religious figure in the district and puts him in the chariot before doing the next thing. Zeal that wants a passenger is performance. Nobody genuinely burning for the honour of God arranges a witness first.

Where the commission ended (vv. 11-14). The house of Ahab, and then his great men and his close friends and his priests — a social circle, not a dynasty — and then forty-two men of the royal family of Judah met by accident on a road, who did not know what had happened and answered his question openly. No word from God anywhere covers that, and the writer records it in the same flat voice and lets it accumulate.

The losses begin (vv. 32-33). Elisha wept in Damascus over what Hazael would do, and here it starts: the whole Transjordan, a third of the kingdom, never recovered. And the first part of Israel to go is Gilead — the hill country a man came out of to tell Ahab there would be no rain except by his word.
10.examples:
Then: The great families of Samaria, who had been bringing up seventy royal children in their own houses, received a letter in the morning and sent the heads to Jezreel the same day — and the man who wrote the letter stacked them in two piles at the town gate overnight and asked the crowd at dawn who could possibly have done it.

Now: Three things. First, verses 28 and 29 together. Ask which of your sins you are willing to be publicly severe about, and notice how reliably it turns out to be one that costs nothing to renounce and that the people around you already disapprove of. The one that needs attention is the one that is holding something up. Second, verse 16. If you find yourself wanting a particular person to be present while you do the right thing, stop there — come with me and see my zeal is not a sentence a zealous man needs to say. Third, the double verdict. Being right about the cause has never yet licensed the conduct, and this chapter is as plain a case as Scripture gives of a man rewarded for what he did and judged for how he did it.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family.<sup>2</sup>But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were being put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Thus they hid him from Athaliah, so that he was not put to death.<sup>3</sup>And he remained with her six years, hidden in the house of the LORD, while Athaliah reigned over the land.<sup>4</sup>But in the seventh year Jehoiada sent and brought the captains of the Carites and of the guards, and had them come to him in the house of the LORD. And he made a covenant with them and put them under oath in the house of the LORD, and he showed them the king's son.<sup>5</sup>And he commanded them, "This is the thing that you shall do: one third of you, those who come off duty on the Sabbath and guard the king's house<sup>6</sup>(another third being at the gate Sur and a third at the gate behind the guards) shall guard the palace.<sup>7</sup>And the two divisions of you, which come on duty in force on the Sabbath and guard the house of the LORD on behalf of the king,<sup>8</sup>shall surround the king, each with his weapons in his hand. And whoever approaches the ranks is to be put to death. Be with the king when he goes out and when he comes in."<sup>9</sup>The captains did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded, and they each brought his men who were to go off duty on the Sabbath, with those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath, and came to Jehoiada the priest.<sup>10</sup>And the priest gave to the captains the spears and shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of the LORD.<sup>11</sup>And the guards stood, every man with his weapons in his hand, from the south side of the house to the north side of the house, around the altar and the house on behalf of the king.<sup>12</sup>Then he brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. And they proclaimed him king and anointed him, and they clapped their hands and said, "Long live the king!"<sup>13</sup>When Athaliah heard the noise of the guard and of the people, she went into the house of the LORD to the people.<sup>14</sup>And when she looked, there was the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!"<sup>15</sup>Then Jehoiada the priest commanded the captains who were set over the army, "Bring her out between the ranks, and put to death with the sword anyone who follows her." For the priest said, "Let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD."<sup>16</sup>So they laid hands on her; and she went through the horses' entrance to the king's house, and there she was put to death.<sup>17</sup>And Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD's people, and also between the king and the people.<sup>18</sup>Then all the people of the land went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And the priest posted watchmen over the house of the LORD.<sup>19</sup>And he took the captains, the Carites, the guards, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD, marching through the gate of the guards to the king's house. And he took his seat on the throne of the kings.<sup>20</sup>So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to death with the sword at the king's house.<sup>21</sup>Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign.
11.overview:
Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, hears that her son is dead and destroys the royal family of Judah — her own grandchildren — to take the throne. This is the one occasion in the history of either kingdom on which anyone attempted to extinguish the line of David, and everything God had promised ran through the children in that room.

One was got out. Jehosheba, a daughter of the royal house and (Chronicles tells us) the wife of the high priest, walked into the massacre and took a one-year-old — and had the presence of mind to take his nurse as well. He spent the next six years in a bedroom off the temple courts, in the one building in Jerusalem that a Baal-worshipping queen had no reason to enter.

In the seventh year Jehoiada swears the captains in the temple and shows them the boy, uses the Sabbath changeover so that twice the usual number of armed men can stand about without comment, and arms them with David's own dedicated spears and shields off the temple wall. The child is crowned and given the law; Athaliah walks in on the noise, cries treason, and is taken out to die away from holy ground; the house of Baal in Jerusalem is pulled down by ordinary people; and a seven-year-old sits on the throne of David.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — She Destroyed All the Royal Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family (v. 1) — her own grandchildren, to take the throne of Judah. One was got out: Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were being put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom (v. 2). And he remained with her six years, hidden in the house of the LORD, while Athaliah reigned over the land (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the only occasion in the history of either kingdom on which anyone tried to extinguish the line of David, and it was attempted by Ahab's daughter. Everything God had sworn — the throne, the seed, the one who would crush the serpent's head — ran through the children in that room. For six years there was no son of David on David's throne, and Jezebel's daughter ruled in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.examples: And notice where the lamp was. Not extinguished — in a bedroom off the temple courts, with a nurse, for six years. Athaliah worshipped Baal and had no reason to go into the house of the LORD, and the one building in the city she never entered was the one with the heir in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family. But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were being put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Thus they hid him from Athaliah, so that he was not put to death. And he remained with her six years, hidden in the house of the LORD, while Athaliah reigned over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family.'

Read that as slowly as it deserves. She destroyed all the royal family — which means her own grandchildren, in her own house, in an afternoon.

Her son had reigned one year and been shot in a chariot on his way home from a family visit in the north. She was the queen mother, a Sidonian by descent, the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, and she had been in Jerusalem more than twenty years. When the news came, she did not mourn and she did not retire. She had every remaining heir of the house of David put to death and took the throne.

Now understand what was at stake in that room, because it is the largest thing in the book.

God had sworn to David that his house and his kingdom would be made sure forever and his throne established forever (2 Sam. 7:16). Every promise in Scripture about a coming king ran through those children — back to a word in Eden about the offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent's head (Gen. 3:15), forward to a birth in Bethlehem. Two chapters ago the writer said the only reason Judah still existed was that God promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever (8:19).

Here is Jezebel's daughter, methodically putting out the lamp.

For six years there was no descendant of David on the throne of David. A woman who worshipped Baal ruled in Jerusalem, and as far as anyone in the city knew, the line was finished.

'But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were being put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Thus they hid him from Athaliah, so that he was not put to death.'

One woman, and the whole of it turns on her.

Jehosheba is a daughter of the royal house — Joram's daughter, Ahaziah's sister, and therefore either Athaliah's daughter or her stepdaughter. Chronicles adds the detail that changes everything: she was the wife of Jehoiada the priest (2 Chron. 22:11). The royal family and the priesthood were joined in one marriage, which is why what happens next is possible at all.

Look at what she actually did. Stole him away from among the king's sons who were being put to death. She went into the room where it was happening, while it was happening, and took one out.

Then the detail that shows a mind working clearly inside a catastrophe: him and his nurse. She took the baby and the woman who could feed him. A one-year-old hidden without a wet nurse would have been dead in three days, and somebody, in the middle of a massacre, thought that through.

'And he remained with her six years, hidden in the house of the LORD, while Athaliah reigned over the land.'

Six years in the temple precincts.

Picture the practicalities, because they are the point. A boy from one to seven, living in rooms attached to the house of God, never outside, never in the street, never seen by anyone who might mention it. A handful of people knew — a priest, his wife, a nurse — and none of them told anyone for six years, which is a very long time to hold a secret in a city that size.

Note why it worked. Athaliah worshipped Baal. She had a temple of her own in Jerusalem, and no reason whatever to walk into the house of the LORD, and she did not. The one building in the capital she never entered was the building with the heir in it.

Set the two pictures against each other and leave them. On the throne, a queen who had killed every child she could find. In a back room a few hundred yards away, a lamp that had been promised to a man dead for a century and a half, still burning, being fed by a nurse.

God's promises are not usually kept the way we would keep them. There was no army, no angel, no thunderclap. There was a woman with enough nerve to walk into that room, a wet nurse who could be trusted, a priest with a spare bedroom, and six years of nobody saying anything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–12 — The Spears and Shields That Had Been King David's
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest brings the captains of the guard into the temple, puts them under oath, and he showed them the king's son (v. 4). The plan uses the Sabbath changeover, when both shifts are present and twice the usual number of armed men can be in the courts without comment (vv. 5-9). Then a detail worth stopping on: the priest gave to the captains the spears and shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of the LORD (v. 10). The guard forms up across the whole width of the building, and the boy is brought out, crowned, given the testimony, anointed and proclaimed (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Six years of holding a secret, and then a plan built entirely out of the ordinary rota. The one day of the week when nobody would ask why there were so many soldiers about is the day he picks, and the men are sworn in the temple in front of the child so that every one of them has seen the reason with his own eyes before he agrees to it.
verseByVerse.examples: And they arm them with David's trophies. Those spears and shields had been taken in David's own wars and dedicated in the house of the LORD (cf. 2 Sam. 8:7), and they come off the wall to be carried by the men standing round the last living descendant of the man who won them.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the seventh year Jehoiada sent and brought the captains of the Carites and of the guards, and had them come to him in the house of the LORD. And he made a covenant with them and put them under oath in the house of the LORD, and he showed them the king's son. And he commanded them, "This is the thing that you shall do: one third of you, those who come off duty on the Sabbath and guard the king's house (another third being at the gate Sur and a third at the gate behind the guards) shall guard the palace. And the two divisions of you, which come on duty in force on the Sabbath and guard the house of the LORD on behalf of the king, shall surround the king, each with his weapons in his hand. And whoever approaches the ranks is to be put to death. Be with the king when he goes out and when he comes in." The captains did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded, and they each brought his men who were to go off duty on the Sabbath, with those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath, and came to Jehoiada the priest. And the priest gave to the captains the spears and shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of the LORD. And the guards stood, every man with his weapons in his hand, from the south side of the house to the north side of the house, around the altar and the house on behalf of the king. Then he brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. And they proclaimed him king and anointed him, and they clapped their hands and said, "Long live the king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But in the seventh year Jehoiada sent and brought the captains of the Carites and of the guards, and had them come to him in the house of the LORD. And he made a covenant with them and put them under oath in the house of the LORD, and he showed them the king's son.'

Six years, and then he moves.

Consider what those six years cost him. He is the high priest of a nation whose throne is occupied by a Baal-worshipping usurper, and he has the rightful king asleep down the corridor, and every day he does nothing about it. He waits until a boy is old enough to stand up in public and be crowned, and until he has judged the loyalty of the men he will need.

When he does move, note the order of the meeting: oath first, then the child. He binds them, in the temple, and then he opens a door and shows them a seven-year-old.

Every one of those officers is going to risk his life on the strength of having seen the boy with his own eyes.

'And he commanded them, "This is the thing that you shall do: one third of you, those who come off duty on the Sabbath and guard the king's house'

'(another third being at the gate Sur and a third at the gate behind the guards) shall guard the palace.'
