'And the two divisions of you, which come on duty in force on the Sabbath and guard the house of the LORD on behalf of the king,'

'shall surround the king, each with his weapons in his hand. And whoever approaches the ranks is to be put to death. Be with the king when he goes out and when he comes in."'

The detail is dull to read and it is the reason the thing works.

He picks the Sabbath, and he picks it because that is changeover day. The shift going off and the shift coming on are both in the temple at once, which means twice the normal number of armed men can be standing in those courts without a single person in Jerusalem thinking it odd.

He is not relying on a miracle. He is using the rota.

There is a kind of faith that thinks planning is a failure of trust. This chapter is one of the places the Bible quietly disagrees. A man who has waited six years for God to keep a promise spends the last week of it working out shift patterns and gate assignments, and the promise is kept through the shift patterns.

'The captains did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded, and they each brought his men who were to go off duty on the Sabbath, with those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath, and came to Jehoiada the priest.'

'And the priest gave to the captains the spears and shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of the LORD.'

Stop here, because this is the loveliest verse in the chapter.

Those weapons had been David's. They were the spoil and the ceremonial arms of his own campaigns — when he defeated Hadadezer, David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem (2 Sam. 8:7) — and they had hung in the house of the LORD as dedicated trophies for a century and a half. Nobody had expected to use them.

They come down off the wall and are put into the hands of the men who will stand round the last living descendant of the man who carried them.

David's own spears, guarding David's last son, in the house David wanted to build, to keep alive the promise David was given.

'And the guards stood, every man with his weapons in his hand, from the south side of the house to the north side of the house, around the altar and the house on behalf of the king.'

A line of armed men right across the width of the temple, from one wall to the other, with the boy behind it.

'Then he brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. And they proclaimed him king and anointed him, and they clapped their hands and said, "Long live the king!"'

Two things are put on him, and the second is as important as the first.

The crown, and the testimony — almost certainly a copy of the law, which Deuteronomy requires every king of Israel to write out for himself and keep beside him and read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God (Deut. 17:18-20).

Crown and book together. That is what makes a king in Israel and not merely a ruler: authority in one hand and a text over him that he did not write and cannot amend.

Athaliah had the throne for six years and never had that. It is the whole difference between the house of David and the house of Ahab.

Then the sound: hands clapping, and men shouting long live the king at a seven-year-old who six days ago had never been outside.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Athaliah hears the noise and walks into the temple, and sees the thing she believed she had destroyed standing by the pillar with a crown on: and Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, Treason! Treason! (v. 14). Jehoiada has her taken out through the horses' entrance — let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD — and killed there (vv. 15-16). Then a covenant, in two directions: between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD's people, and also between the king and the people (v. 17). The people pull down the house of Baal in Jerusalem and kill its priest (v. 18), the boy is seated on the throne, the city is quiet — and Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Treason, from the woman who murdered the royal family in order to take the throne. It is the usurper's word, and she is the only person in the building with no right to use it.
verseByVerse.examples: And the reform goes further than a change of ruler. There was a house of Baal in Jerusalem — Athaliah had built her mother's religion into the capital of Judah — and it comes down in the same week, so that within a few years of each other Baal is put out of both kingdoms. What makes it more than a coup is verse 17: they are bound to God first, and then to one another.

verseByVerse.quote: When Athaliah heard the noise of the guard and of the people, she went into the house of the LORD to the people. And when she looked, there was the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!" Then Jehoiada the priest commanded the captains who were set over the army, "Bring her out between the ranks, and put to death with the sword anyone who follows her." For the priest said, "Let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD." So they laid hands on her; and she went through the horses' entrance to the king's house, and there she was put to death. And Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD's people, and also between the king and the people. Then all the people of the land went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And the priest posted watchmen over the house of the LORD. And he took the captains, the Carites, the guards, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD, marching through the gate of the guards to the king's house. And he took his seat on the throne of the kings. So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to death with the sword at the king's house. Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Athaliah heard the noise of the guard and of the people, she went into the house of the LORD to the people.'

She walks into the temple.

Six years she has ruled this city without setting foot in that building, because it was not her god's house and she had a house of her own for him. And the first time she goes in, it is because of a noise she cannot account for.

'And when she looked, there was the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!"'

And when she looked, there was the king.

She had counted the bodies. She had made certain, six years ago, in a room in her own palace, and she had been queen ever since on the strength of it. And there he is by the pillar, in the place where kings of Judah stood, crowned, with the trumpets going and the whole city cheering.

Then she says the one word she has no right to. Treason.

The woman who murdered her own grandchildren to seize a throne that was never hers stands in the temple and accuses everybody else of it. That is not an unusual sound. People who have taken something are frequently the loudest about theft, and they are not being cynical when they say it; they have been in possession long enough to feel robbed.

'Then Jehoiada the priest commanded the captains who were set over the army, "Bring her out between the ranks, and put to death with the sword anyone who follows her." For the priest said, "Let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD."'

In the middle of a coup, with the woman who destroyed the royal family standing in front of him, the priest stops to give an instruction about where she may be killed.

Let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD.

That is restraint of a rare kind. Everything is going his way; the guard is his, the city is his, the king is crowned, and nobody would have said a word if she had been cut down where she stood. And he takes the trouble to have her walked out first, because the house of God is not a place for that, even for her, even now.

Jehu, in the north, killed a temple full of men and turned the building into a latrine, and God gave him four generations. Jehoiada, in the south, will not have one guilty woman executed on holy ground. Both were doing God's work; only one of them was careful.

'So they laid hands on her; and she went through the horses' entrance to the king's house, and there she was put to death.'

She dies at the horses' entrance of the palace.

Her mother died in a gateway in Jezreel with her blood on the wall and the horses trampling over her. The writer does not draw the line, and it may be nothing. But the two women who brought Baal into two kingdoms both died in a gateway among horses, twenty-five miles and a few years apart.

'And Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD's people, and also between the king and the people.'

Two covenants, and this is what raises the day above a palace coup.

The first is vertical: the LORD, the king and the people, that they should be the LORD's people. That is the Sinai formula being taken up again by a nation that had spent six years under a Baalist queen — we are yours.

The second is horizontal: between the king and the people. The seven-year-old is bound to them and they to him. Judah has just watched what happens when a ruler is accountable to nothing, and the answer is an agreement in both directions before the boy has been on the throne an hour.

'Then all the people of the land went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And the priest posted watchmen over the house of the LORD.'

There was a house of Baal in Jerusalem.

Let that land. Athaliah had not merely taken the throne of David; she had built her mother's religion into the capital of Judah, with a temple and altars and images and a named priest, within sight of the house of the LORD. That is what one marriage alliance, made in a spirit of family friendship two generations earlier, had grown into.

It comes down in an afternoon, torn apart by the people of the land — not by the guard and not by decree, but by ordinary Judeans who had evidently been waiting a long time for permission.

Within a few years of each other, Baal has now been put out of both kingdoms: by a soldier in the north, by a congregation in the south.

'And he took the captains, the Carites, the guards, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD, marching through the gate of the guards to the king's house. And he took his seat on the throne of the kings.'

They walk him down from the temple to the palace under guard, and a child sits down on the throne of David.

'So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to death with the sword at the king's house.'

'Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign.'

End on that sentence, because the writer does.

Seven years old. The entire weight of every promise God ever made about a king from David's line — the throne established forever, the offspring of the woman, the one whose kingdom would have no end — rested that morning on a boy who had spent six of his seven years in a back bedroom of the temple and had never seen the city he was king of.

Nine hundred years later another child of that line was carried out of reach of a king who was killing children, by relatives who moved at night, and kept alive in obscurity until it was safe (Matt. 2:13-16). The pattern is not accidental. Twice the promise came down to one infant and a family willing to hide him, and both times the people trying to put the light out did not know which room to look in.

One honest word before leaving him. This boy will do well for as long as Jehoiada lives, and after the old priest dies he will listen to different men, and he will have Jehoiada's own son stoned to death in the temple court (2 Chron. 24:20-22). The rescue in this chapter was real and God's promise was kept, and the child who was saved grew into a man who needed saving from himself. That is not a flaw in the story. It is why the line had to keep going.

11.theology:
What was at stake (v. 1). The throne established forever (2 Sam. 7:16), the offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent's head (Gen. 3:15), and the lamp the writer named two chapters ago as the only reason Judah still existed (8:19) — all of it ran through the children Athaliah had killed. For six years there was no son of David on David's throne and Jezebel's daughter ruled in Jerusalem.

How the promise was actually kept (vv. 2-3). No army, no angel, no sign. A woman with the nerve to walk into the room while it was happening; the presence of mind to take the wet nurse as well, without whom a one-year-old would have been dead in three days; a priest with a spare bedroom; and six years of a handful of people saying nothing. God keeps his word through means, and the means are usually somebody's courage and somebody else's competence.

The rota (vv. 5-9). Jehoiada picks the Sabbath because both shifts are present and the courts can be full of soldiers without anyone thinking it strange. There is a piety that treats planning as a failure of trust; a man who had waited six years for God to keep a promise spent the last week of it on gate assignments, and the promise came through the gate assignments.

David's weapons (v. 10). Spoil from David's own wars, dedicated in the house of the LORD (cf. 2 Sam. 8:7) and hanging there unused for a century and a half, taken down and put into the hands of the men guarding David's last descendant.

Crown and testimony (v. 12). He is given the law along with the crown, as Deuteronomy requires of a king (Deut. 17:18-20) — authority in one hand and over him a text he did not write and cannot amend. Athaliah held the throne for six years and never had that, and it is the whole difference between the house of David and the house of Ahab.

Not in the house of the LORD (v. 15). Everything is going Jehoiada's way and nobody would have objected, and he stops the execution long enough to have her walked outside. Jehu killed a temple full of men and made the building a latrine; Jehoiada will not have one guilty woman put to death on holy ground. Both were doing God's work and only one was careful.

Two covenants (v. 17). Vertical first — the LORD, the king and the people, that they should be the LORD's people — and then horizontal, between the king and the people. That is what lifts the day above a palace coup, and it is the answer of a nation that has just watched what a ruler accountable to nothing does.
11.examples:
Then: A woman walked into the room where her family's children were being killed, took one of them out, and remembered to take the wet nurse too — and then a priest, his wife, and a nurse kept a boy alive in a back bedroom of the temple for six years without one of them ever mentioning it.

Now: Three things. First, the shape of the rescue. If you are waiting for God to keep a promise, notice that in the largest such moment in the Old Testament he used a brave sister-in-law, a nurse, a spare room and a duty roster, and that from inside those six years it must have looked exactly like nothing happening. Second, Jehoiada's planning. The man had a divine promise, a rightful king and a usurper on the throne, and he spent his last week on shift patterns; treating careful preparation as a failure of faith is a piety this chapter does not share. Third, Athaliah's cry. Treason was shouted by the one person in the building with no right to the word — and she almost certainly meant it, because six years of possession is long enough to feel robbed of something you stole.
